prevent the Fund and its Customers, governing bodies and service providers from being misused for ML/TF or any other
financial misconduct or crime.
The Fund is only allowed to invest in countries included in the DAC List of ODA Recipients, who also qualify against the
Jurisdictional Eligibility Criteria (“JEC”) policy of the Fund, and subject to Advisory Board approval. This UNSC requirement
can be formally built in to the JEC monitoring process if required. No individual or entity that is listed on any UN Security
Council sanctions list, including the UN Consolidated Sanctions list will be involved in any manner with the project or its
activities, either as a counterparty, implementer, or beneficiary.

Selected Risk Factor 12
Category Probability Impact
Changed credit environment High Low
Description
Risk that the terms offered to investors no longer remain attractive and reasonable given a changed credit environment.
Mitigation Measure(s)
Very limited funding has been mobilized overall from private sector investors to date into the necessary paradigm
shift of commodity supply chains sourcing sustainably from tropical forest regions. A primary objective of the &Green
Fund is exactly to change that; the proposed programme has been designed and operates in a way that specifically
intends to remove these barriers, by providing solid returns in the form of coupons that are competitive.
Project investments are structured with considerable downside protection, and substantial first loss protection that
the Tranche A investors (including GCF) provide, which changes the risk adjusted return perception of the targeted
private sector investors. This is a necessary step for building the blueprints that establish investor confidence in the
space through a blended finance approach.
The coupons offered to investors (including Tranche A investors via the catch up) will depend on the exact timing
of the offering and interest rate levels at that time. The coupons offered are commensurate to the risk profile of a
private sector investor in this debt fund, and should not be compared to double-digit returns expected from private
equity (impact) funds. We have not had any feedback in our private sector investor discussions on a concern over
the interest rates offered, key issues are the right “fit” in terms of structure and the extent of downside protection.
On the asset side, &Green does not provide loans to its investees (borrowers) that are concessional in pricing. The
concessionality comes from structuring the loans in a way that is currently not available on the market, including
longer tenors and principal grace periods, but interest rates are at levels that are in line what a purely commercial
investor would require in order to support the blueprinting nature of the &Green programme.
The pricing of both the funding from senior loans and the interest which &Green can charge to its borrowers is
referenced to the long term risk free rate (e.g. 10 year SOFR).
As interest rates rise, long-term fixed rate capital such as that provided by &Green, is increasingly sought after. We
expect increased interest in the &Green offering for this reason, as well as because of increasing regulatory pressure
to implement no-deforestation strategies.
We have not seen a deterioration of the credit quality of the borrowers in the &Green portfolio due to the changing
market environment. &Green performs quarterly valuations of its portfolio that have to be approved by the &Green
board, and no material change was noted in the last assessment. A high-level summary of this assessment is
provided as a supportive document. &Green uses an Expected Credit Loss (ECL) model for this purpose that has
been approved by the &Green Board, and the &Green auditor (PWC), based on the &Green Impairment Policy.

GCF POLICIES AND STANDARDS
G.1. Environmental and social risk assessment (max. 750 words, approximately 1.5 pages)
317. Environmental and social risk classification: The proposed programme is expected to have positive
environmental and social impacts as it delinks deforestation from commodity supply chains and builds climate
resilience through the implementation of sustainable agricultural practices. The programme requires large agri-
commodity producers to commit to “No Deforestation, No Peatlands, No Exploitation” (NDPE) practices. Despite
the expected positive impacts, the overall environmental and social risk rating for this project is “high”, according
to the GCF Environmental and Social Safeguards requirements (Category I-1).
318. Environmental and Social Management System: The &Green Fund is committed to integrating
environmental and social considerations and will operate an Environmental and Social Management System
(ESMS) throughout the programme. This is operationalised at the investment level through environmental and
social due diligence; risk assessment; and establishment of a management framework tailored to the nature and
scale of the activities and the magnitude of environmental and social risks and impacts associated with each
investment. The ESMS has been designed in accordance with IFC Performance Standard 1 as well as best
practices of ESG management for funds, such as those provided by CDC Group, FMO, the GCF and IUCN. For
efficiency, the ESMS is digital, and incorporates a system of continuous improvement.
319. Framework approach for risk mitigation: The framework of the ESMS includes the following set of tools
used to establish appropriate Environmental and Social Action Plans (ESAPs) for each investment:
• Policies - describing the requirements and objectives relating to No Deforestation, No development of
Peatlands, No Exploitation (NDPE) and Landscape Protection Plans (LPP)
• Frameworks – including Forest and Biodiversity Framework and the Key Performance Indicator (KPI)
Framework
• Templates
320. &Green Fund’s approach is determined by applying best practice criteria and requirements based on identified
risks to investments during due diligence. The following categories are subject to screening and due diligence, with
IFC PS, UNGP, applicable legislation and frameworks serving as references: Health, safety and labour related
issues of investees, gender- and labour-related issues of investees, communities and social conflicts,
displacements and settlements, Indigenous People, Human rights and its diverse aspects (Indigenous People,
Communities, Labour issues, Child/slave work, gender issues including SEAH). In case of any material findings,
the mitigation/remediation measures become part of ESAP. If a material risk is identified, either a second stage of
focused due diligence is undertaken, or an action plan to address the risks elaborated and implemented. Further
details of the ESMS framework can be found in Annex 6, with details on analysed issues in item 3.2. of the Annex.
321. Stakeholder engagement: &Green Fund has undertaken a thorough stakeholder engagement process at
programme level and requires stakeholder engagement for each sub-project investment. &reen Fund maintains a
Complaint Management policy that provides easy and clear access to all stakeholders, both local and international.
One member of the &Green Board, rather than SAIL Ventures, is dedicated to receiving and managing complaints.
SAIL Ventures, as the investment manager contracted to operate the Fund will be the global focal point for &Green.
Sail Ventures has resources in Southeast Asia and in Latin America and additional in-country resources will be
added via GCF support for Component 2. For more information, see the accompanying &Green Complaints
Management Policy (Annex 6, Appendix 3). An effective grievance mechanism is required of investees as
prescribed by the Stakeholder Engagement process (Annex 7). Grievance redress for stakeholders is subject to
due diligence as per IFC PS requirements. The stakeholder engagement process is fully integrated in the
investment process of &Green Fund.
322. In order to enable Transformational Change, maximize positive impacts and mitigate E&S risks, &Green Fund
employs forms of local stakeholder engagement throughout the investment management process. When assessing
the transformational potential of transaction, &Green Fund engages with its local partners (e.g. IDH) in order to
map potentially relevant stakeholders. These stakeholders may enable the transformational change in the
landscape, thus their engagement may be considered as an element of LPP later on. They may include local
farmer’s associations, non-profits, governmental bodies, research institutes etc.
323. Impact assessment: The &Green Fund assesses and manages social and environmental impacts of its
(future) investments. The ESMS system operates on two levels - jurisdictional and transactional - and is fully

integrated in the investment process of the Fund, from the development of the investment rationale until the exit

• the Transformational Change Assessment Phase, described in an Investment Rationale;
• the Screening Phase, which is documented in a Deal Note and includes macro processes of Defining the
Scope, E&S Risk Screening (including Reputation Screening, Forest & Biodiversity Screening and Gender
Screening including SEAH) and Risk Categorization, detailed in Annex 6, item 3.2.;
• the LPP Design, which is documented in the Credit Application and comprises due diligence (ESDD), ESAP
that contains TC and risk-related milestones, impact targets, IFC PS matrix, detailed in Annex 6, item 3.3.
324. The E&S screening phase aims to identify main material risks. In addition to the identified stakeholders, &Green
Fund screens those actors that should be considered both in due diligence and LPP design phases from the risk
understanding/mitigation perspective (e.g. NGOs, local associations and similar).
325. The due diligence scope is defined by the screening results, but depending on the severity of findings, &Green
Fund may consult some local actors (e.g. research institutions, civil rights organizations, certification bodies and
similar) in order to better scope the third-party due diligence process. During the due diligence, third party decides
on necessary stakeholder engagement to investigate, provide dimension and mitigation options for the E&S risks.
For the biodiversity-related risks, third party follows the requirements of Terms of Reference as per &Green Fund’s
Forest and Biodiversity Framework, including for the level of stakeholders consultations and engagement – these
stakeholders may become part of stakeholder engagement by client in future LPP, if relevant. Due diligence related
gender issues, including SEAH, the third party follows the guidelines of Gender Framework and use respective
ToR.
326. Information disclosure requirement: The Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) was
translated and disclosed in Bahasa Indonesia, English, French, Lao, Malay, Portuguese, Spanish, and Vietnamese
on the &Green Fund and FMO websites as of 17 June 2022. Physical copies will be made available in each country
as investments are made in the jurisdictions, as well as where registered offices of the executing entities exist.
G.2. Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
327. Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Action Plan informs the programme’s design as presented in this Funding
Proposal. The overall objective of the gender assessment is to provide a baseline understanding of the
opportunities to engage in gender-transformative investment through the &Green Fund structure. It also aims to
screen, analyze and mitigate SEAH risks, in adherence to the IFC Performance Standards that are embedded
within the investment process. The following two standards are of relevance:
328. Performance Standard 2, paragraph 15: on Non-discrimination and Equal opportunity, therefore committing to
take measures to prevent and address harassment, intimidation, and/or exploitation, especially in regard to women
329. Performance Standard 4, paragraph 1: committing to avoid or minimise the risks and impacts to community
health, safety, and security that may arise from project related-activities, with particular attention to vulnerable
groups.
330. The assessment integrates in-depth analysis of gender-based inequalities and SEAH-related risks that exist in
the countries (via country-specific gender profiles), the context and sociocultural factors underlying gender
inequality that are exacerbated by climate change and optimize the potential contributions of women and men of
all ages to build both individual and collective resilience to climate change. This assessment will be used to inform
project-level formulation, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation.
331. The Gender Action Plan (GAP) has been designed to ensure, through designated actions, that the challenges
faced by women and vulnerable groups in accessing and benefiting from the proposed programme, if financed by
the GCF, are meaningfully addressed. The GAP describes gender-related activities, baselines, sex-disaggregated
indicators and targets, roles and responsibilities, and financial and human resources.
332. Due to pandemic-related restrictions, this gender assessment has been prepared using a combination of
primary information and data available to &Green Fund on the target countries, especially through the extensive
Jurisdictional Eligibility Criteria Approach (JECA) process, and secondary information and literature collected via
an in-depth desk review. The literature review focused on gender mainstreaming, deforestation, climate change
and value chains as a broader topic
333. The &Green Fund recognizes that gender mainstreaming132 is both necessary and relevant for the programme
to maximise its outcomes for no deforestation. This assessment, therefore, focuses on &Green Fund’s internal

integrated in the investment process of the Fund, from the development of the investment rationale until the exit
evaluation. The following sections describe each step in the investment process in more detail:
• the Transformational Change Assessment Phase, described in an Investment Rationale;
• the Screening Phase, which is documented in a Deal Note and includes macro processes of Defining the
Scope, E&S Risk Screening (including Reputation Screening, Forest & Biodiversity Screening and Gender
Screening including SEAH) and Risk Categorization, detailed in Annex 6, item 3.2.;
• the LPP Design, which is documented in the Credit Application and comprises due diligence (ESDD), ESAP
that contains TC and risk-related milestones, impact targets, IFC PS matrix, detailed in Annex 6, item 3.3.
324. The E&S screening phase aims to identify main material risks. In addition to the identified stakeholders, &Green
Fund screens those actors that should be considered both in due diligence and LPP design phases from the risk
understanding/mitigation perspective (e.g. NGOs, local associations and similar).
325. The due diligence scope is defined by the screening results, but depending on the severity of findings, &Green
Fund may consult some local actors (e.g. research institutions, civil rights organizations, certification bodies and
similar) in order to better scope the third-party due diligence process. During the due diligence, third party decides
on necessary stakeholder engagement to investigate, provide dimension and mitigation options for the E&S risks.
For the biodiversity-related risks, third party follows the requirements of Terms of Reference as per &Green Fund’s
Forest and Biodiversity Framework, including for the level of stakeholders consultations and engagement – these
stakeholders may become part of stakeholder engagement by client in future LPP, if relevant. Due diligence related
gender issues, including SEAH, the third party follows the guidelines of Gender Framework and use respective
ToR.
326. Information disclosure requirement: The Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) was
translated and disclosed in Bahasa Indonesia, English, French, Lao, Malay, Portuguese, Spanish, and Vietnamese
on the &Green Fund and FMO websites as of 17 June 2022. Physical copies will be made available in each country
as investments are made in the jurisdictions, as well as where registered offices of the executing entities exist.
G.2. Gender assessment and action plan (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
327. Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Action Plan informs the programme’s design as presented in this Funding
Proposal. The overall objective of the gender assessment is to provide a baseline understanding of the
opportunities to engage in gender-transformative investment through the &Green Fund structure. It also aims to
screen, analyze and mitigate SEAH risks, in adherence to the IFC Performance Standards that are embedded
within the investment process. The following two standards are of relevance:
328. Performance Standard 2, paragraph 15: on Non-discrimination and Equal opportunity, therefore committing to
take measures to prevent and address harassment, intimidation, and/or exploitation, especially in regard to women
329. Performance Standard 4, paragraph 1: committing to avoid or minimise the risks and impacts to community
health, safety, and security that may arise from project related-activities, with particular attention to vulnerable
groups.
330. The assessment integrates in-depth analysis of gender-based inequalities and SEAH-related risks that exist in
the countries (via country-specific gender profiles), the context and sociocultural factors underlying gender
inequality that are exacerbated by climate change and optimize the potential contributions of women and men of
all ages to build both individual and collective resilience to climate change. This assessment will be used to inform
project-level formulation, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation.
331. The Gender Action Plan (GAP) has been designed to ensure, through designated actions, that the challenges
faced by women and vulnerable groups in accessing and benefiting from the proposed programme, if financed by
the GCF, are meaningfully addressed. The GAP describes gender-related activities, baselines, sex-disaggregated
indicators and targets, roles and responsibilities, and financial and human resources.
332. Due to pandemic-related restrictions, this gender assessment has been prepared using a combination of
primary information and data available to &Green Fund on the target countries, especially through the extensive
Jurisdictional Eligibility Criteria Approach (JECA) process, and secondary information and literature collected via
an in-depth desk review. The literature review focused on gender mainstreaming, deforestation, climate change
and value chains as a broader topic
333. The &Green Fund recognizes that gender mainstreaming132 is both necessary and relevant for the programme
to maximise its outcomes for no deforestation. This assessment, therefore, focuses on &Green Fund’s internal

Gender Approach and the operationalization of gender mainstreaming within its institutional investment
management structure (see Section 3 – Annex 8). Embedding gender into deforestation commitments offers
considerable opportunities for leveraging synergies between restoration goals, climate change adaptation as well
as mitigation action and global commitments to sustainable development goals - SDGs (particularly SDG 5 –
Gender Equality; SDG 8 – Decent Work; SDG 12 – Sustainable Production and Consumption; SDG 13 – Climate
Action; and SDG 15 – Life on Land).
334. The key issues identified in the Annex 8 are:
• Participation of women in forestry management is inextricably tied to the social, cultural, historical, and
political contexts of communities where forest management efforts take place. Gender plays a key role in
shaping environmental rights of control, access, and responsibility that interact with class, race, caste,
culture, or ethnicity to shape ecological change and sustainable livelihoods. (Peach Brown, 2011)133
• Strategies for increased participation of women in commercialized and well-developed supply chains
(particularly export-facing ones) require upgrading based on the typology of the women in question. While
women in female headed households may require limited efforts such as tailoring financial products to their
needs or providing interlinked services coupled with prompt payment for their produce to allow them to
produce quality fruits and access lucrative markets, women in male-headed households need
institutionalization of gender-sensitive policies in the governance of producer groups to enable them to
upgrade as value chain integrators and value chain owners. (CGIAR, 2017)134
• Informal economies and markets are the dominant source of livelihoods in rural areas – and the
engagement in forestry value chains is often crucial for rural women’s livelihoods and the well-being of their
household. (IIED, 2015)135
• Women’s time poverty and physical safety concerns limit their access to and use of forest resources and
related activities. (CIF, 2017)136
• See Annex 8, Section 2.3 for more information.
335. The Fund will take the following approach to address these issues:
• The &Green Fund’s Gender Approach will provide a framework to accelerate gender-transformative and
gender-sensitive (as appropriate for each Deal) investments through the &Green Fund structure.
• The Gender Approach will be mobilized through the Environment and Social Action Plans (ESAPs) – which
are strict environmental and social safeguarding covenants that are conditions of the loan contracts of the
&Green Fund. The Gender Analysis has influenced the overall logical framework (in Section E of this
Funding Proposal) and has identified entry points for the chosen paradigm shift pathway to deliver gender
and social co-benefits, which will be detailed project-level investment stage, as reflected in the Gender
Action Plan.
Gender mainstreaming through the TAF:
336. The &Green TAF was formally launched in 2019 through a Cooperation Agreement with IDH, and aims to
reduce risk and maximise the impact of the &Green Fund (potential) investment projects, by supporting investment-
readiness, monitoring, post-investment client support and sharing of lessons and knowledge from &Green Fund
and its investment projects with third party stakeholders. IDH is the service provider of the &Green TAF.
337. IDH has identified that equitable and meaningful participation of women as key to driving sustainable
intensification and growth in trade, although gender barriers remain rife in commodity supply chains. To address
this concern, IDH has developed a Gender Toolkit, consisting of practical case examples from IDH and similar
projects in congruent sectors, and a Gender Guide, where opportunities to integrate gender aspects in different
programming steps of projects and inventions are explored. The &Green Fund’s Gender Approach will employ
these existing and field-tested tools.
338. The role of the TA Facility in gender mainstreaming is both to enhance understanding of gender dynamics in
the early project cycle, and to maximize opportunities for enhanced gender equality and empowerment. By
considering how women and men participate in interventions, the TA Facility enables the &Green Fund’s
investments to promote and contribute to gender equality. This can include technical assistance to ensure
substantial and impactful participation by women in stakeholder consultation processes, in the project

G.3. Financial management and procurement (max. 500 words, approximately 1 page)
Financial management
339. The detailed provisions regarding financial management of GCF resources by the AE will be described in the
FAA. Periodic reporting will be provided by FMO to the GCF specifying among others:
● The amounts already committed and disbursed by &Green Fund by country and by project;
● The amounts already committed and disbursed by IDH by country;
● The remaining amount on different GCF accounts;
● A provisional disbursement schedule on a one-year rolling horizon;
● For the loan component, a list of the incidents recorded during the repayment period of the loan provided to
project clients.
340. FMO is already an investor in &Green Fund and has completed AML/CFT and KYC checks on Stichting
AndGreen.Fund. Subsidiary agreements regarding management of GCF resources will be signed between FMO
and &Green Fund. The EE is required under the FAA and Term Sheet to carry out AML, CFT and KYC checks on
recipients of GCF resources in line with FMO standards. Credit risk monitoring of project borrowers will be carried
out by &Green Fund through the assessment of the financial statement of the borrowers, monitoring of financial
covenants, etc. Audits will be requested and performed as per FMO’s internal guidelines.
Disbursement
341. At FMO level, disbursement will concern investment into &Green Fund on behalf of GCF whose disbursement
will be reported to FMO. Disbursement by the &Green Fund to loan recipients will follow the procedures and
requirements described in the Term Sheet.
Procurement
342. FMO’s procurement rules are in line with international standards and have been reviewed by GCF as a
condition of accreditation, the policies and obligations of which will be passed down to the EE. The procurement
plan at programme level is provided in Annex 10.

Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment of
FP212
Proposal name: &Green Fund: Investing in Inclusive Agriculture and Protecting
Forests
Accredited entity: Nederlandse Financierings-Maatschappij voor
Ontwikkelingslanden N.V. (FMO)
Project/programme size: Large
I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1.1 Overview
1. This is the second submission of the full proposal “&Green Fund: Investing in
Inclusive Agriculture and Protecting Forests” to the independent Technical Advisory
Panel (iTAP). The accredited entity (AE) is the Nederlandse Financierings-Maatschappij
voor Ontwikkelingslanden N.V. (FMO).
2. This full proposal aims at contributing to low-carbon, climate-resilient development
pathways by lowering investments’ risk while promoting zero-deforestation, socially
inclusive commodity production.
3. The iTAP considered in its assessment all documents as submitted on 18 April 2023,
the answers to iTAP’s questions as received on 16 May 2023, the responses during the
Q&A session on 17 May 2023 and the amended documents received by iTAP on 23 May
2023 as a result of minor revisions agreed between iTAP and the AE during the Q&A
session. These minor revisions will avoid misunderstandings when implementing the full
proposal. The iTAP acknowledges the constructive response from the AE to the
comments, concerns and recommendations expressed by iTAP during the first
submission.
4. Commodity production is an important driver of deforestation in the tropics. This is
true for several commodities including palm oil, soybeans and beef. The funding proposal
is aimed at making possible to scale-up an existing investment facility (&Green Fund),
which already promotes deforestation-free and socially inclusive commodity supply
chains (e.g. palm oil, cocoa, rubber, cattle).
5. FMO, as the AE, requests GCF support to transform major tropical commodity supply
chains to be deforestation-free and socially inclusive in a way that is commercially viable
and replicable at scale. This paradigm shift assumes that (a) sustainable intensification of
commodity production will reduce extensification (i.e. deforestation) while securing
socioeconomic and adaptation co-benefits and (b) the willingness to invest in sustainable
intensification of agricultural commodity production in the tropics is a consequence of
how private investors perceive its financial risks. The &Green Fund will develop
blueprints for sustainable commodity supply chains that other players can replicate
and/or scale-up in future.
6. Today, several barriers make it difficult to put sustainable commodity supply chains
in place: (a) limited capital flows in sustainable intensification due to high risk perception
by private investors; (b) market distortions that undervalue standing forests and induce
deforestation; (c) limited local access to knowledge and technology for no-deforestation

=== PAGE 125 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 121
production; (d) inaccessible or poorly presented information on climate hazards and
adaptive measures; and (e) insufficient regulatory or policy conditions that support
sustainable practices and environmental impact.
7. The &Green Fund seeks to overcome these barriers by making deforestation-free
commercial agriculture and forestry a profitable and viable alternative and setting the
stage to drive sustainable land use investment at scale. The GCF investment should reduce
private investments’ risks in zero-deforestation commodity supply chains, while
improving enabling conditions and capacities in the given areas (countries or subnational
entities).
8. The funding proposal covers Brazil, Cameroon, Colombia, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic
Republic of the Congo, Ecuador, Gabon, Indonesia, Lao People’s Democratic Republic,
Liberia and Zambia. The starting point for any transaction is the identification of
commodity supply chains currently identified as drivers of deforestation in the specific
areas (country or subnational level) and could evolve into sustainable production using a
method developed by &Green Fund: the Jurisdictional Eligibility Criteria Assessments
(JECA).
9. The funding proposal is structured around two components: (1) the &Green Lending
Facility; and (2) the Technical Assistance Facility (TAF). The &Green Lending Facility
(component 1) responds to barrier (a) (see para. 6 above) and aims to result in the
creation of a scalable investment vehicle (B.V.);1 the mobilization of co-investment by the
private sector; and fund capital disbursed to large-scale sustainable agriculture
transactions. The TAF (component 2) will address barriers (b) to (e) and aims to result in
policy dialogue and awards raising; technical cooperation for capacity-building of
companies and businesses in the supply chain; and a monitoring, reporting and
verification system that allows for paradigm shift tracking.
10. It is expected that the GCF investment will facilitate the mitigation and adaptation
impacts of the programme. Based on results from investments over the past four years,
FMO, the AE, expects an investment lifetime impact of approximately 350,000 tonnes of
carbon dioxide equivalent (t CO eq) in greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction and removals per
2
USD 1 million invested. This results from emissions reduction from avoided deforestation
in &Green Fund’s protected forests, which will be monitored using a combination of
satellite data and national forest reference emission levels/forest reference levels
(FRELs/FRLs). The AE expects that a total investment of USD 960 million over the
investment lifetime (15 years) will result in a contribution to climate change mitigation of
circa 340 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (Mt CO eq).
2
11. Further, the AE expects to contribute to the GCF results areas on health and well-
being, food and water security, and ecosystems and ecosystem services. Based on &Green
Fund’s existing portfolio, and aligning with the GCF impact framework, the programme is
expected to yield the following adaptation metrics:2
(a) Over 15.7 million hectares of land under sustainable and resilient management; and
(b) At minimum, 2,000 people with enhanced resilience per USD 1 million invested (a
USD 960 million investment for 1,900,000 people).
12. The targeted size of the programme is USD 981,620,000. The requested contribution
from GCF is USD 189.35 million, out of which USD 180 million is in the form of a loan and
1 The acronym B.V. comes from the Dutch term besloten vennootschap met beperkte aansprakelijkheid
2 The initial estimates for people with enhanced resilience were conservatively calculated due to limited data, extrapolating
from the existing portfolio and considering the pipeline of investments. Results during implementation are expected to be
higher than these estimates.

USD 9.35 million is in the form of a grant. The rest of the co-funding will be secured over
the project length from third parties.
1.2 Impact potential Scale: High
13. The iTAP assessment is guided by decision B.33/12, which explains the principles for
demonstrating the impact potential of GCF-supported activities, as well as other appraisal and
assessment guidance for this investment criteria and as approved by the GCF Board.
Mitigation potential
14. The AE expects a contribution to the climate change mitigation results area on forestry
and land use of 340 Mt CO eq over the investment lifetime (15 years). This is an
2
indicative figure. Detailed calculations will be done for each jurisdiction (i.e. for each
transaction) over the project life using methods available to iTAP for assessment.
15. The funding proposal presents a comprehensive methodological approach. It describes
three types of mitigation contributions: (1) avoided deforestation in forests protected by
&Green incentives; (2) avoided deforestation in forests in supply sheds (landscapes) of
&Green influence; and (3) forest restoration in forests protected by &Green incentives.
Further, the proposal considers potential GHG emissions increments resulting from land
management activities. This allows identifying relevant, project related emissions from
intensification of agriculture and livestock management, with especial consideration of
methane (CH ) and nitrous oxide (N O).
4 2
16. For all above-mentioned types of mitigation contributions as well as for assessing
potential increases of emissions due to land management intensification, the funding
proposal includes a corresponding quantification approach. For each quantification
approach, the funding proposal includes examples based on ongoing activities by &Green
Fund.
17. That said, the mitigation contribution to the forestry and land use results area mentioned
in paragraph 14 above only includes contribution type 1 (avoided deforestation in forests
protected by &Green incentives). The other two mitigation types are quantified in order
to understand and monitor further mitigation contributions but are not accounted for.
This increases the conservativeness of the overall quantification approach.
18. The &Green Fund will continue working in sectors that are known as drivers of
deforestation and will design programmes to overcome barriers at a company and supply
chain-specific level at the deforestation frontier. National FRELs/FRLs will be assessed
across jurisdictions and will be considerably lower than rates of forest loss in areas highly
exposed to agri-commodity expansion. Thus, as far as the programme implementors have
full control of the jurisdiction and no other activities will occur in the area, the application
of FREL/FRL approaches by &Green in at-risk supply chains can be considered as
conservative.
19. The funding proposal states that the &Green Fund will incentivize the avoidance of
deforestation through the:
(a) Protection of identified forest areas (and avoidance of deforestation) as part of
contractual covenants; and
(b) Intensification of agricultural production while reducing incentives and demand for
extensification, thereby avoiding deforestation. While the specific number of hectares
of avoided deforestation are not explicitly identified, the expected impact can
nonetheless be estimated.

=== PAGE 127 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 123
20. The funding proposal includes a quantification method for avoided deforestation
(hectares) and emissions reduction (type 1):
(a) From FRLs, the deforestation rate in percentage (% per year) for the relevant biome
is extracted from the FRL deforestation rate in proportion to the areas of relevant
forest;
(b) The deforestation rate for the reporting year (e.g. 2021) in relevant jurisdictions per
transaction (in % per year) is established using satellite imagery;
(c) FRL and satellite deforestation rates are compared and a demonstrably conservative
value (in % per year) is selected;
(d) The % deforestation rate is applied to &Green’s “forest protected” areas to estimate
avoided deforestation per year;
(e) The area of avoided deforestation is multiplied by the emission factors from the FREL
to quantify emissions reduction; and
(f) The satellite analysis is undertaken and reported annually.
21. During the first submission of this full proposal, iTAP expressed the need to clarify how
the specific projects within &Green Fund can establish the deforestation threat at the
project level in order to attribute the emission reduction to changes in the production of a
particular commodity in a specific place (attribution). The iTAP considers that especially
relevant for calculating GHG emission reduction using the method presented above. As a
response, the AE included a clarification about how this attribution is conducted along the
five for the JECA assessment, as part of the investment rationale, during the Deal Note,
during the credit application, and once included in the &Green Fund portfolio.
22. The second mitigation contribution type is emissions reduction from avoided
deforestation using a marginal production approach. It assumes that intensification of
agricultural production reduces the demand for extensification. The corresponding ten-
step method is described in the proposal. Complementing this approach and in response
to the iTAP recommendations during the first submission, the AE now incorporates a
protocol for assessing the materiality of potential sources emissions increases within the
investment boundaries (annex 22e).
23. Annex 22e explains (i) the rationale and approach to assessing, quantifying and reporting
individual source emissions increases; (ii) the implications of source emissions increase
in the context of investment emissions impacts; (iii) relevant standards, methodologies,
resources and literature used; and, when relevant, (iv) how source emissions are included
in measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) protocols and incorporated into
&Green’s operational procedures. The annex includes a threshold for identifying the
materiality of the source emissions increases (25,000 t CO eq/year) and a safeguard
2
regarding impact magnitude related to the total size of the mitigation potential of a given
investment.
24. The third type of mitigation contribution is removal estimates for the enhancement of
carbon stocks in remaining forest and through reforestation. The accounting method
applies a simple approach of RF multiplied by the area of forest restoration. RFs are
extracted from relevant FREL/FRLs from national governments for appropriate forest
types or biomass when available. When RFs are not available from FRELs, they are
conservatively established from Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
factors appropriately selected for biomass growth, ratio, and carbon fraction in
accordance with approaches used in FREL/FRLs and national GHG accounting.
25. The success of the activities related to climate change mitigation depends upon the level
of control of the land (i.e. clarity of land tenure and land use rights). The AE explained that

=== PAGE 128 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 124
land tenure issues are included in the Landscape Protection Plans (LPP) and
Environmental and Social Action Plans (ESAP) of each transaction. The AE further
clarified that in the initial screening of a transaction, the land rights situation is assessed
as part of the first risk assessment. For due diligence, a full environmental and social
impact assessment will also be carried out, including a detailed assessment against the
International Finance Corporation (IFC) Performance Standards (PS) on environmental
and social sustainability, specifically standard 5 “Land Acquisition and Involuntary
Resettlement”.
26. The iTAP considers that the methodological approach presented by &Green Fund is
complete, coherent and allows for proper MRV over time. This methodological approach
is based on sound scientific and non-scientific knowledge and experience. The iTAP
recognizes that the operationalization of this methodological approach will be challenging
in some of the countries where the &Green will operate and is aware of the importance of
the Technical Assistance Facility (TAF) included as component 2 of the proposal for facing
these challenges.
Adaptation potential
27. During the first assessment of this full proposal, iTAP recommended the development of
a methodological approach for assessing adaptation potential at the project level. In the second
submission, the AE includes an additional annex explaining the &Green approach to climate risk
assessment and the identification, planning, implementation and monitoring, reporting and
verfitication of adaptation actions.
28. In order to mainstream adaptation to climate change in its operations, the &Green Fund
will follow a climate risk management process incorporated into the screening, due diligence
and loan tenor for all investments (see figure 1 below).
29. The process proposed by &Green Fund includes the following eight steps:
1) Define scope of assessment and economic activity (as of lending scope), including
considerations about business (sector), geographic jurisdictions and locations
included in the loan and time span (10 years as default for the investment and up to
2050 for the future climate);
2) Define relevant lifespan of the components of the economic activity, differentiating
between investments with relatively short asset lives (<10 years) that will be affected
by the “current” climate and those with long asset lives (>10 years) that will be
affected by the current and future climate;
3) Determine investment components (assets, services, functions), which are material
to the relevant economic activities. These will include areas of agricultural land with
intensified practices, areas of protected forest as well as farmers and communities
associated with these lands. In this step it will be assessed where there is dependence
on individual suppliers for which a climate risk assessment should be conducted
(procurement climate risk assessment). Similarly, when transportation is relevant for
the investment (e.g. between production and market sites), transportation routes will
be included as part of the climate risk assessment whenever alternate routes are not
viable;
4) Screen climate hazards: identify relevant hazards from prescribed lists, which are
based on the European Union taxonomy.3 This screening step will allow, for each
3 European Union taxonomy of ‘climate-related hazard’ from Delegated Regulation 2021/2139, Annex I, Appendix A, and
related to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change:
https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_Chapter12.pdf.

=== PAGE 129 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 125
investment, the filtering out of hazards not relevant for the country or region, hazards
not relevant (i.e. no exposure) at the site, and hazards that will not affect the assets;
Figure 1: &Green’s climate risk assessment process
Source: Funding proposal
5) Climate risk assessment through (a) understanding the significant relationships
between climate hazards and investment components; (b) gathering information on
current and future climate hazards; (c) gathering information on sensitivity and
adaptive capacity of potentially affected components and assessing vulnerability; and
(d) collating and presenting the analysis. The assessment will facilitate the
understanding of climate impact chains (cascade effects). Climate hazard assessments
are taken for < 10 years (with ‘current climate’ as a proxy), and for > 10 years (using
representative concentration pathways (RCP) 8.5 scenarios). If country-specific,
region-specific or site-specific data/models are available, these will be used. For this
step, the proposal refers to the resources available at www.climateinformation.org,
which is co-funded by GCF. Other available tools and sources of information are
included in the full proposal as well. The annex further explains how to assess the
vulnerability of the relevant assets and clarifies how sensitivity, exposure and
adaptive capacity are to be included as part of this step. As outcome of this step is
becomes clear which assets of the investment are under which climate risk and if this
risk is low, medium or high, or if an activity becomes a maladaptation.
6) Prepare adaptation solutions based on the conclusions of the steps above a project
will identify potential actions to reduce hazards and/or vulnerability, and/or increase
resilience for the identified material risks; assess the feasibility of potential actions
and select the most viable; and prepare a concrete adaptation plan and the
corresponding monitoring plan to be included in the MRV of the whole investment;
7) Documentation and verification will be conducted along the whole process in order
to facilitate the evaluation of climate change adaptation progress as well as learning
within the specific project and in the whole &Green Fund community;
8) Update and continuous improvement, based on the update/repeat and reassessment
of climate risk, will be conducted. Its frequency will fit the loan tenor and needs but is

=== PAGE 130 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 126
expected every 3 years for <10-year hazards and at the midpoint of tenor, but not
more than every 6 years (maybe <10 update at year 3 and at year 6). In response to
these updates, adaptation plans will be revised when needed.
30. Steps 1, 2 and 3 will be included during the preparation phase above; step 4 will be part of
the identification of relevant hazards and vulnerability; step 5 will be included as a risk assessment;
step 6 will be included as adaptation solutions; step 7 will be conducted for monitoring and
verification purposes along the whole process; and step 8 promotes adaptive management through
a learning effect between the MRV and repeated identification of hazards and vulnerability over
time.
31. The full proposal includes examples of how to operationalize the whole methodological
approach for climate change adaptation using real situations from existing investments, as well
as a list of input resources that can be useful when operationalizing the methodological
approach.
32. The full proposal also explains how the monitoring and reporting of climate impacts and
adaptation solutions is included in the overall framework for key performance indicators, in the
investment process of &Green Fund and in the operational manual.
33. The iTAP considers that the methodological approach now included in this full proposal
is aligned with the principles as established in decision B.33/12 and that it makes a good use of
existing knowledge and available tools. As with the methodological approach for assessing,
monitoring and reporting the mitigation potential, iTAP considers it extremely important to
include support and capacity-building/capacity transfer for using this methodological approach
as part of the activities in component 2 of the full proposal the Technical Assistance Facility
(TAF).
1.3 Paradigm shift potential Scale: Medium to high
34. The funding proposal presents a good overview of the drivers of deforestation in the
selected countries: Brazil, Indonesia, Cameroon, Colombia, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic
Republic of the Congo, Ecuador, Gabon, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Liberia and
Zambia.
35. Further, it documents scientific outputs regarding climate risks, impacts, adaptation and
mitigation interventions and benefits related to seven commodities: palm oil, livestock
farming/cattle, soy, rubber, coffee, cocoa and timber. The scientific references combine
meta-analysis studies and case studies. Case studies refer to the selected countries as well
as to other countries in the tropics.
36. This information, combined with the generic barriers presented in the funding proposal,
explains the need to tackle commodity supply chains as a main driver of deforestation in
the tropics and why it is so important to involve the private sector in a transformative
process.
37. The funding proposal assumes that lowering the investment risks for private investors
can contribute to the transformation of the commodities supply chain and, consistent with
this assumption, the &Green proposal aims to establish blueprints for financing
deforestation-free commodity production that is commercially viable and replicable.
38. The starting point for the investments is an assessment at the national or subnational
level against five jurisdictional eligibility criteria established by &Green Fund, which allow
for the identification of promising opportunities at the jurisdictional level.
39. This &Green eligibility assessment uses the following criteria:

=== PAGE 131 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 127
(a) Scope: The amount and quality of forest/peatland potential is significant and highly
relevant from a global perspective;
(b) Ambition and strategy: There is a clear strategy with the targets tracking the
reduction of deforestation against historic trends in the jurisdiction. Continued
jurisdictional eligibility is dependent on subsequent biennial positive assessments of
progress;
(c) Timely progress towards milestones indicated in the strategy of the jurisdiction on a
trajectory towards the targets for reducing deforestation;
(d) A transparent MRV system is operational and able to monitor, measure, report and
verify reduction in deforestation and, where relevant, forest and peat degradation in
the jurisdiction; and
(e) Social and environmental safeguards: Progress shown towards the implementation of
the Cancun Agreement.
40. This overall approach for identification, selection and investment support has been used
by &Green Fund since its creation in 2017. Currently, &Green Fund has seven transactions
in its portfolio: three in Brazil, three in Indonesia and one in Colombia. The portfolio
investments account for USD 142.75 million.
41. Currently, &Green Fund manages around USD 180 million, with key investors including
Norway’s International Climate and Forest Initiative (NICFI), FMO, Unilever, the United
Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (through the FMO-managed Mobilising
Finance for Forests programme), the Global Environment Facility (GEF), and the reinsurer
Hannover Re.
42. The proponents expect that co-investment from the private sector will be triggered by
GCF participation and will be secured from commitments made by potential investors to
scale capital disbursements to borrower companies. For the funding proposal, the overall
amount (GCF + co-financing) is expected to be USD 981,620,000, meaning an expected co-
funding of over USD 750,000,000. This growth in co-funding will indeed mark success in
terms of scalability and can be considered a good proxy for assessing paradigm shift. This
approach that links continuing GCF support to demonstrated mobilization impacts is
proper and better aligns GCF paradigm shift interests to the actual execution of the
&Green Fund.
43. The repeatability and scalability of the blueprints developed by &Green Fund depend
upon two main factors: the extent to which the blueprints can be repeated for new
commodities and in new countries and the level of success in mobilizing co-funding,
especially from the private sector. In addition, national conditions and regulations for
loans vary significantly among the 11 countries included in the proposal, and mobilizing
private investments in zero-deforestation, resilient and inclusive agriculture has proven
to be challenging.
44. A mitigating uncertainty on this funding proposal’s overall potential for paradigm change
is whether this programme can lead to changing how financial markets as a whole
approach agriculture and supply chain finance. The transactions in the current &Green
Fund portfolio are with major agricultural market players who typically do not struggle to
access finance for overall operations. It is significant that the concessionality provided
here could lead these entities towards more sustainable practices, but it is not clear
whether the incentives are in place for further market uptake by other sources of finance.
Conversely, there may be a risk that other commercial sources of finance would begin to
compete on financing terms without additional sustainability obligations being attached.

=== PAGE 132 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 128
45. Thus, the paradigm shift depends upon the willingness of big players in the agro-industry
to stop deforestation in areas they could use for commodity production. As most of these
players have access to funding in their own countries, key questions remain open: How
will this programme encourage a paradigm change in a market where finance sources are
accessible for big commodity producers without considering deforestation? Why will
commodity producers prefer loans from &Green? What is the expected impact on or
reaction from other providers of finance? Is there some evidence of factors towards
structural change in any of the countries &Green Fund has worked with since 2017?
46. The iTAP acknowledges the clarifications given by the AE during the second submission
with respect to market availability of loans as offered by &Green and the attempts to
collaborate with local banks to structure co-financing transactions. However, iTAP
considers that the challenges remain. It does not mean that the proposal needs to change;
it only implies that all participant organizations should be aware of the challenges and is a
further argument supporting GCF involvement.
1.4 Sustainable development potential Scale: High
Alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals:
47. The funding proposal contributes indirectly to almost all of the Sustainable Development
Goals (SDGs), but contributes most directly to:
(a) Goal 8 (Decent work and economic growth) through the reduction of investment
risks in sustainable commodity production in the tropics using a socially inclusive
and gender-sensitive approach (SDG 5);
(b) Goal 12 (Responsible consumption and production) through the transformation of
commodity production through scaling up the sustainable production of agricultural
commodities;
(c) Goal 13 (Climate action) through the expected GHG emission reductions from
avoided deforestation as well as carbon enhancement from restoration and the
expected increase in climate resilience among the beneficiaries and ecosystems; and
(d) Goal 15 (Life on land): Although the proposed programme does not account for
biodiversity benefits, it is well accepted that halting deforestation and reversing land
degradation have a positive effect on biodiversity conservation.
48. In addition, iTAP considers that the funding proposal has high potential to contribute to
SDG 6, especially target 6.6, by protecting and restoring water-related ecosystems.
Social and environmental co-benefits:
49. &Green Fund presents its approach towards social and environmental co-benefits in its
investment principles and environmental and social management system (ESMS) manual.
The manual provides the approach towards securing social and environmental co-benefits
during the planning and implementation of projects receiving loans, as presented in the
paragraphs below.
50. &Green adopts the IFC PS as its framework for managing environmental and social risks
and impacts associated with the projects it seeks to finance. These include PS 1:
Assessment and Management of Environmental and Social Risks and Impacts; PS 2: Labor
and Working Conditions; PS 3: Resource Efficiency and Pollution Prevention; PS 4:
Community Health, Safety, and Security; PS 5: Land Acquisition and Involuntary
Resettlement; PS 6: Biodiversity Conservation and Sustainable Management of Living
Natural Resources; PS 7: Indigenous Peoples; and PS 8: Cultural Heritage.

=== PAGE 133 ===
GCF/B.36/02/Add.07
Page 129
51. Additionally, &Green Fund requires its clients to obtain the free, prior and informed
consent of all local communities (not just indigenous peoples) with customary rights to
land used for both production and conservation components of projects that &Green Fund
finances.
52. For the financing of small and medium-sized enterprises, including smallholders and
smallholder cooperatives, other local or international standards (e.g. Roundtable on
Sustainable Palm Oil – Principles and Criteria in the case of the palm oil sector), including
those developed specifically for smallholders, may be used where the PS are equivalent
but may be more familiar to or better adapted to the scale and intensity of management of
the client.
53. The IFC PS may be used in conjunction with relevant best practice standards, guidelines
and tools (such as the Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of
Land, Fisheries and Forests in the Context of National Food Security; Sustainable
Agriculture Standard; Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil – Principles and Criteria; Forest
Stewardship Council Principles and Criteria; High Carbon Stock Approach Toolkit;
Climate, Community and Biodiversity Standards; or other emerging best practice
standards), where these provide additional detailed guidance or requirements that
support compliance with the IFC PS.
54. Considering the importance of biodiversity-related impacts in its investments, &Green has
a specific process that mainstreams biodiversity concerns into investment decision-
making: the Forest & Biodiversity Framework. The framework embeds PS 6 within
&Green’s ESMS and provides guidance on the biodiversity-specific studies commensurate
with the level of biodiversity risk presented by the investment to provide a pragmatic
approach for balancing cost-effective risk management while maintaining the integrity of
the PS.
55. Moreover, &Green Fund requires clients to make an unconditional written organizational
policy commitment to no deforestation, no development of peatlands, and no exploitation
(NDPE). The &Green Fund monitors progress on the NDPE policy commitments
throughout the tenor of its investments.
56. &Green also requires clients to translate their vision for maximizing long-term
environmental impacts and social inclusion and for contributing to sector transformation
into Landscape Protection Plan (LPP) and to commit to its implementation as part of its
investment. The LPP describes a client’s strategy and the additionality of the strategy
against sector practices in the landscape in which they operate.
Gender-related co-benefits
57. The funding proposal includes (i) a comprehensive gender assessment and gender action
plan developed following the GCF manual Mainstreaming Gender in Green Climate Fund
Projects; and (ii) a logical framework showing the consideration of gender aspects at the
outcomes and outputs level.
58. The gender assessment and gender action plan include an assessment of the current
gender situation in 17 countries,4 a gender-differentiated summary of pre-selected sectors
in these 17 countries and a gender-differentiated short analysis of the links to four SDGs
(SDG 1 on poverty, SDG 3 on health, SDG 4 on education and SDG 8 on decent work and
economic growth).
59. It also presents the ‘green gender approach’, which consists of two different tracks
(gender-sensitive and gender-transformative) and shows how the ‘green investment
4 With all 11 countries relevant for this funding proposal included.

process’ uses these tracks throughout the stages of the following investment phases:
investment rationale, deal note, credit application and MRV.
60. The iTAP assesses the approach of this funding proposal towards social and
environmental co-benefits and the gender action plan as coherent, consistent and robust.
The iTAP also highlights that achieving the expected environmental and social co-benefits

level of the AE and executing entity (EE).
1.5 Needs of the recipient Scale: High
61. The Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Uses (AFOLU) sector is one of the major sources
of GHG emissions in all 11 countries included in this funding proposal. In all countries,
emissions related to deforestation as a result of commodity production is a major area of
concern, and reducing deforestation is included in the nationally determined
contributions of the participating countries.
62. Similarly, in all countries included in this funding proposal, the increasing vulnerability of
ecosystems, people and agricultural activities due to increasing climate hazards has been
recognized either in the nationally determined contributions and/or in the national
adaptation plans (or corresponding national policies or processes).
63. It is widely recognized that transforming commodity supply chains that are causing
deforestation requires not only enabling conditions but also transforming the economic
rationale along the chain. That requires high investments and competences.
64. This funding proposal suggests an approach to tackle some of the important barriers to
halting deforestation in tropical countries at present, while offering a comprehensive
approach that can serve not only climate action but several other SDGs and respond to the
needs expressed by the recipients at the national level.
1.6 Country ownership Scale: Medium to high
65. As stated above, halting deforestation and reducing climate vulnerability in the
agricultural sector is a priority in the national policies of all 11 countries included in this
funding proposal.
66. The no-objection letters (NOLs) of Brazil, Cameroon, Colombia, Côte d’Ivoire, the
Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic,
Liberia and Zambia were included in the submission assessed by the iTAP. Further NOLs
were in preparation when conducting this assessment.
67. Overall, iTAP positively views the inclusion of the funding proposal’s JECA from a country
ownership standpoint. JECA provides for some level of review and evaluation as to
whether a particular jurisdiction is making progress in reducing deforestation in recent
years; whether systems are in place for tracking forest levels; and the effectiveness of its
environmental and social safeguard framework. Building enabling environment analysis
into financial decision-making around GCF-supported concessionality is important to
demonstrate that supported projects are in jurisdictions that have climate interests
aligned to GCF in practice and not solely on paper.
68. The iTAP also acknowledges the clarification about tailored engagement strategies as part
of the activities in component 2, the Technical Assistance Facility (TAF). However, iTAP
considers that the level of current engagement of subnational authorities responsible for

the subnational authorities responsible for forest conservation is still rather low.
1.7 Efficiency and effectiveness Scale: Medium to high
69. With total financing of USD 981,620,000, this funding proposal expects to have a
mitigation impact of 339,150,000 t CO and benefit 1,963,000 people. This corresponds
2eq
to less than USD 3/t CO eq, which is considered an efficient ratio. However, the actual
2
figure will depend upon success in generating investments by the private sector. The
expected ratio is a USD 3.75 investment by the private sector for each USD 1 invested by
GCF.
70. GCF and the AE, FMO, will contractually agree that GCF will commit USD 189.35 million to
the &Green Stichting5 for the funded activity. GCF will then be an indirect lender to the
&Green Stichting (through FMO in its capacity as a GCF AE).
71. Of the total amount from GCF, USD 750,000 will be provided to &Green Stichting as a non-
reimbursable grant for component 1 (lending facility) and outputs 1.1 and 1.2, and
USD 180 million will be provided to &Green Stichting as a subordinate loan for output 1.3
(investment facility).6 For component 2 (TAF), USD 8.60 million will be provided as a non-
reimbursable grant to &Green Stichting.
72. FMO will make a USD 180.75 million capital commitment to &Green Stichting in the form
of a non-reimbursable grant and a subordinated loan. The Stichting can then remit the full
USD 180 million investment facility to the scalable investment vehicle &Green B.V. (the
"B.V.") as tranche A equity—in the form of the current portfolio assets, cash and undrawn
commitments, and further capital raised by the Stichting to the extent required—for loans
to project companies.
73. The funding proposal suggests three GCF disbursements to FMO (44.67 per cent, 27.66
per cent and 26.66 per cent), subject to conditions stated in the funding proposal.
74. FMO will likewise make a USD 8.6 million capital commitment in the form of a non-
reimbursable grant to &Green Fund for implementing some or all of component 2’s
activities through its existing TAF Cooperation Agreement with IDH,7 the technical
assistance service provider.
75. In order to mobilize further investments, &Green Stichting will incorporate a Dutch

&Green Stichting will provide equity capital to the B.V. (and will be the only equity capital
provider to the B.V.) in the form of the current portfolio assets and further capital raised

instruments (tranche B) in the form of notes to the private sector.

investors in tenor and timing of reflows.
80. Tranche A will act as the principal catalyst to attract commercial capital into the structure
by providing a first-loss buffer to further private sector investors in &Green B.V.

83. Both the Stichting (tranche A) and commercial investors (tranche B) will earn returns
financed by the interest income received from debt investments.
84. Income earned by the &Green B.V. includes interest income from the debt portfolio,
interest income on any term deposits or other short-term savings instruments, and fee
income (including upfront fees and structuring fees).
85. The iTAP values the transparent presentation of the financial structure and the efforts
towards protecting the investments. &Green Fund’s primary efficiency and effectiveness
benefits are derived from its innovative blended financing approach.
86. There are several commendable features in this funding proposal’s approach. The iTAP
finds that conditional disbursements are more effective and efficient. The disbursements
align GCF interests to that of AEs and EEs and also reduce the level of effective
concessionality over time as the GCF tranche shrinks relative to overall financing.
87. Other appropriate and effective features include the transfer of the existing asset at an
amortized par value and the use of a waterfall distribution that permits GCF to achieve
improved returns in the event the programme succeeds. Concessional providers like GCF
are often at risk of over-subsidizing vehicles, thus risking windfall profits for fund
managers and co-investors. For that reason, it is more efficient and effective to have
structures that allow GCF to claw back some additional return in the event the funded
programme performs adequately.
88. The iTAP acknowledges the clarifications and the information provided in the second
submission with regard to progress in securing co-funding. As some of this information is
labelled as confidential, it is not summarized in this assessment. However, the additional
information allows iTAP to assess this progress and therefore rate the efficiency and
effectiveness of this proposal as medium to high depending on the success in finalizing the
co-funding negotiations.

Proposal name: &Green Fund: Investing in Inclusive Agriculture and Protecting Forests

(FMO)
Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
Impact potential Scale: High
AE answers to iTAP comment(s)
Thank you for this assessment, we agree that the impact potential of the &Green Fund is high. The feedback provided
by iTAP in our first submission enabled us to revise existing, and create additional, documentation focused on
explaining the methodological approach to both mitigation and adaptation. We appreciate the review of the revised
Annex 22 and all appendices (22a, b, c, d, e and f) that presents, in detail, the method behind &Green’s impact
calculations.
We have developed and presented additional methodology documents based upon the Panel’s initial feedback to
provide further clarity into adaptation potential at the project level. Further, the development of a detailed
Operations Manual, which has been provided in the second submission to the iTAP, allows for additional
transparency and explanation of the MRV process relating to adaptation actions. We note the Panel’s request for
activities within Component 2 and we share the view relating to the importance of capacity building support.
Paradigm shift potential Scale: Medium to high
AE answers to iTAP comment(s)
Thank you. Commodity players work in very low margin markets, where any changes to sourcing are risky and find
limited appetite from a commercial perspective. Working capital is always a limiting factor for commodity
businesses, and therefore there is reduced appetite to deploy it to make risky changes to the status quo. &Green
provides long-term funding that is adapted structurally to the nature of the paradigm shift the fund finances
– therefore eliminating these risks for the commodity players.
&Green’s early investments have already led to increased interest in &Green in countries of operation to date
(Indonesia, Brazil, Colombia), and increasingly &Green is working with local banks to structure co-financing
transactions. All &Green investments must, at project level, over the duration of the transaction catalyze at least 3x
&Green’s funding, this project level co-financing is in place already for a number of existing investments.
We believe the risk of competing funding without sustainability obligations to be low, as &Green has already, with
the existing portfolio demonstrated, that no compromise on return is necessary while sustainability conditions are
inherently reducing overall investment risk.
The funding &Green provides is not available in the market today, and it is a key objective for &Green to
demonstrate to the financial markets that adapting their funding structures could drive paradigm shift at
scale; the investment process requires detailing of this logic in an increasing level of detail.
Regarding paragraph 46 in ITAP’s assessment relating to the market availability of loans as offered by &Green and
attempts to collaborate with local banks to structure co-financing transactions - this is noted and agreed upon. It is
ultimately the key challenge that this programme seeks to address, together with the structuring of the investment
opportunity to be attractive to mainstream commercial investors. These two key objectives are effectively two
sides of the same coin, and GCF’s catalytical funding will be instrumental to establish the proof of concept at scale.

High

Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
This Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan have been prepared for &Green and FMO by
E Co, to inform the project design of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) Funding Proposal titled:
&Green Fund: Investing in Inclusive Agriculture and Protecting Forests. The proposed project aims
to remove deforestation from major commodity supply chains in a commercially viable and
replicable manner. The aim is to create blueprints for sustainable land use and management that
others in the market can adopt, replicate and scale significantly; thereby making &Green’s and
GCF’s initial investment in the market ‘transformational’.

Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
Glossary
Term Definition
Gender A culturally-defined set of economic, social, and political roles, responsibilities, rights,
entitlements obligations, associated with being female and male, as well as the power relations
between and among women and men, boys and girls. The definition and expectations of what it
means to be a woman or girl and a man or boy, and sanctions for not adhering to those
expectations, vary across cultures and over time, and often intersect with other factors such as
race, class, age and sexual orientation. Transgender individuals, whether they identify as men
or women, are subject to the same set of expectations and sanctions.
(OHA/PEPFAR, modified from the Interagency Gender Working Group – IGWG)
Gender Equity The process of being fair to women and men, boys and girls. To ensure fairness, measures must
be taken to compensate for cumulative economic, social, and political disadvantages that
prevent women and men, boys and girls from operating on a level playing field.
(IGWG training resources)
Gender Equality The state or condition that affords women and men equal enjoyment of human rights, socially
valued goods, opportunities, and resources. Genuine equality means more than parity in
numbers or laws on the books; it means expanded freedoms and improved overall quality of life
for all people. (IGWG training resources)
Gender-blind are project designs and activities that ignore gender factors including roles and relations and
can lead to reinforcement of gender-based discrimination and existing inequities. (USAID)
Gender-balance requires that men and women be equally represented - either in equal numbers or in proportion
to their presence - in particular settings. (USAID)
Gender-sensitive Gender-sensitive investments will acknowledge the different needs and constraints of women
and men without changing the status quo. The client may, for example, realize that the work of
female smallholders in the supply chain is not sufficiently recognized, which limits their access
to training. When providing training to female smallholders, the client could focus on the
activities they perform and attempt to limit the negative effects of a gendered distribution of
responsibilities, such as a heavier workload for women, without challenging the gendered
differences themselves. Gender sensitive approaches can be easily integrated into existing
training structures on other topics since they don’t require underlying gendered behavioral
patterns to be addressed. (adapted from the IDH – Gender Guide)
Gender- Gender-transformative investments will address gender imbalances, changing gendered power
transformative relations, and actively building equitable social norms and structures. An organization is aware
that women and men do not have equal opportunities in the household, at community level or
at work. They may, for example, create equal working conditions for women and men,
recognizing that special means may be required to increase the number of women in
management positions or to achieve an environment free from gender based violence (GBV).
Gender transformative approaches are characterized by explicitly centering gender norms and
are thus common for interventions that have the primary goal of addressing gender issues and
transforming gender relations to promote equality. (adapted from the IDH – Gender Guide).

Mainstreaming administrative functions, as well as into the institutional culture of an organization. This process

Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
1. Introduction to Annex 8
1.1 Programme concept of the &Green Fund
This decade – 2021 to 2030 – marks the ambitious United Nations Decade on Ecosystem
Restoration.1 This will aim to prevent, halt and reverse the degradation of ecosystems – a key
driver of which is combatting deforestation.
Through the timely &Green Fund: Investing in Inclusive Agriculture and Protecting Forest
programme, FMO2 – the Accredited Entity (AE) – along with requested GCF support – will invest in
the &Green Fund3 to mobilise drivers that delink – and ultimately, remove – deforestation from
major commodity supply chains in commercially viable and replicable manner.
To do so, the &Green Fund will scale up commercial investment in tropical agricultural supply
chains while transforming them to be zero deforestation and socially inclusive at a landscape
level. Investments, for the Fund, include those targeting forest and peat conservation and
restoration embedded in landscapes of sustainable and regenerative agriculture. Target sectors,
for the Fund, are the major supply chains driving deforestation, such as: livestock, palm oil, soy,
rubber, cocoa and forestry.
The programme is comprised of two main components (see Section E – Funding Proposal for the
Logical Framework):
Component 1 focuses on the establishment and operation of the investment vehicle (see Section
C.1 – Funding Proposal for details on Fund structure), which will secure co-financing and invest
directly in commodity supply chain businesses that embrace zero-deforestation production and
forest protection.
Component 2 provides a technical assistance facility that overcomes the capacity and information
barriers facing commodity producers and neighboring communities, while building a community
of practice for replication and scale-up for producers as well as incorporating gender-responsive
action in the target countries.
