1.2 Objective of the gender assessment
Given this background, this Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan have been prepared for
FMO, to inform the project design of the GCF Funding Proposal and contribute towards generation
of gender outcomes. It is the Annex 8 of the Funding Proposal and has been developed
according to the guidance provided by the GCF on mobilising gender action through climate
finance, notably through the Mainstreaming Toolkit4.
The overall objective of the gender assessment will be to provide a tool to mainstream and
accelerate gender-responsive and gender-transformative investment through the &Green Fund
structure.
Within the overarching objective, the Gender Assessment will have two outcomes: to integrate an
analysis of gender-based inequalities that exist in the countries, the context and sociocultural
factors underlying gender inequality which are exacerbated by climate change and optimize the
potential contributions of women and men of all ages to build both individual and collective
resilience to climate change. Therefore, this assessment will be used to inform project
formulation, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation.
Lastly, the assessment will inform the Gender Action Plan (GAP). The GAP has been designed to
ensure, through designated actions, that the challenges faced by women and vulnerable groups in
accessing and benefiting from the proposed programme, if financed by the GCF, are meaningfully
addressed. The GAP will contain gender-related activities, baselines, sex-disaggregated indicators
and targets, roles and responsibilities, and financial and human resources.
The &Green Fund recognizes that that gender mainstreaming5 is both necessary and relevant for
the programme to maximise its outcomes for zero deforestation. This assessment, therefore,
details &Green Fund’s internal Gender Approach and how it aims to bolster gender mainstreaming
within its institutional structure (see Section 3). The assessment will also ensure that gender-
responsive processes (including robust gender analysis, including assessment of SEAH-related risks,
indicator selection, outcome mapping, monitoring and evaluation) are formalized within the
external investment thesis of the &Green Fund (see Section 3). Embedding gender into
deforestation commitments offers considerable opportunities for leveraging synergies between
restoration goals, climate change adaptation as well as mitigation action and global commitments
to sustainable development goals - SDGs (particularly SDG 5 – Gender Equality; SDG 12 – Sustainable
Production and Consumption; SDG 13 – Climate Action; and SDG 15 – Life on Land).

1.3 COVID-19: the pandemic’s gendered effect on
livelihoods
During the development of this assessment, the global community continues to grapple with
COVID-19, which is wreaking havoc on the lives of millions of people, both with regard to health
and wellbeing, and socioeconomic indicators. Despite deforestation slowing down during the initial
stage of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the planet still lost around 4.2 million hectares (according
to Global Forest Watch) of primary tropical forest that year, an area the size of the Netherlands.
A large proportion of this loss was driven by agriculture, both smallholder and large-scale
commodity cultivation. This forest loss is a major reason why agriculture accounts for one-quarter
of all greenhouse gas emissions.

2.2 Applying concurrent triangulation to identify gender
barriers for the &Green Fund
The study employs a concurrent triangulation methodology, and deliberately sidesteps
sequential research processes. In sequential designs, either the qualitative or quantitative data
are collected in an initial stage, followed by the collection of the other data types during a
succeeding, second stage.15 In contrast, concurrent designs are characterized by the collection of
both types of data during the same stage (which was the case for the development of this
assessment).16
Within these two categories, there can be three specific designs based on:
(a) the level of emphasis given to the qualitative and quantitative data (equal or unequal),
(b) the process used to analyze and integrate the data, and
(c) whether or not the theoretical basis underlying the study methodology is to bring about social
change or advocacy.17
Since the secondary research was formative in nature and rapid in mandate (to cover all 17 target
countries), the assessment necessitated a prompt methodology to establish an inventory of
information and a gender baseline that can be operationalized to cover the complex aspects of
deforestation, value chains, and climate change.
Therefore, the concurrent approach is suited because of: the flexibility to use secondary
quantitative and qualitative findings for the comprehension of the studied phenomenon in the
primary research (mainly through existing &Green work), and the accuracy it can provide to
samples of intermediate or small size. This also ensures that the assessment and action plan are
able to propose measures that are relevant for the delivery of outputs identified in the results
framework.
15 Creswell JW, Plano Clark VL, Gutmann ML, Hanson WE. Advances in mixed methods research designs. In: Tashakkori
A, Teddlie C, editors. Handbook of mixed methods in social and behavioral research.

3. Introduction to the &Green Fund
3.1 Lending Philosophy
The &Green Fund’s lending philosophy conceptualizes and demonstrates to both public and private
actors on how to provide for inclusive economic growth, and forest and peat protection (and
potentially restoration) when financing the production of agricultural commodities that are
sourced from tropical landscapes. It does so by:
• Providing credit facilities only in jurisdictions with progressive forest and/or peat
protection agendas and sustainable development strategies.
• Adding quantitative output-based environmental and social criteria and targets to the
financing of commodity production.
• Improving livelihoods of smallholders by including them in high-productivity, sustainable
supply chains.
• Attracting commercial investors into such projects by partly mitigating their credit risk
(financial) and environmental risk (sustainability safeguarding).
• Stimulating innovation in business models and approaches to catalyse financially
sustainable, deforestation free, socially inclusive, high productivity agriculture in tropical
forest landscapes.
• Offering tailored debt instruments, such as: extended tenor, subordination in order to
stimulate co-investment from the market, where the market does not or will not at this
time invest alone.
The &Green Fund, especially on land and forest governance, supports and requires its investees
to engage with communities and local, regional and national governments. These engagements
are often enabled by its long-term supply chain and landscape convening partner IDH18, and its
clients’ partner implementing organisations on the ground in the majority of &Green target
regions.
3.2 Theory of Change (ToC)
The ToC of the &Green Fund ensures there is increased gender mainstreaming and social inclusion
through the fund structure. This is because &Green’s financial and technical support aims to level
the playing field for sustainable, climate resilient and deforestation-free agriculture. The Fund
provides risk capital to new commodity production systems; incentivises the intensification of
agricultural production without increasing deforestation; helps commodity producers price the
externalities provided by natural forests; reinforces public policy signals and encourages improved
regulation; and motivates mainstream private sector investors to provide increased capital inflows
at scale for responsible producers.
18 Translated from the original Dutch: “Initiatief voor Duurzame Handel” (IDH)

This will have a direct impact on improved livelihoods – which can have a positive impact on
household performance. Further, by stemming deforestation, the Fund will mitigate long-term
climate impacts, which will reduce the exposure of vulnerable communities (particularly in
tropical contexts) – as well as marginalized groups within these communities (often, women or
Indigenous Peoples).

3.3 Internal Standards
The &Green Fund provides flexible, needs-adapted structures to finance commodity supply chain
investments in &Green’s approved jurisdictions, all of which have progressive forest and/or
peatland protection strategies & policies. Each investment must, at initial screening stage,
demonstrate transformational change potential, and provide substantial environmental returns.
Therefore, &Green has an internal, embedded standard of ‘do no harm’ which can be mobilized
towards mainstreaming a gender-aware perspective throughout the Fund structure. Examples from
other tools include:
3.3.1 Exclusion List
The &Green Fund’s Exclusion List identifies stringent measures to preclude any business portfolios
that include:
• Forced labour or child labour – as defined by International Labour Organization standards
• Activities or materials deemed illegal under host country laws or regulations or
international conventions and agreements, or subject to international phase-outs or bans
• Cross-border trade in waste and waste products, unless compliant to the Basel Convention
and the underlying regulations
• Destruction of High Conservation Value areas
• Radioactive materials and unbounded asbestos fibres
• Pornography and/or prostitution
• Racist and/or anti-democratic media
• In the event that any of these following products form a substantial part of a project’s
primary financed business activities: alcohol beverages; tobacco; weapons and munitions;
and/or gambling, casinos and equivalent enterprises.
3.3.2 Jurisdictional Eligibility Criteria Assessment (JECA)
The &Green Fund catalyses investment into jurisdictions where local and host government
authorities are also committed to reducing deforestation, and are actively taking steps to work
with the private sector, communities and civil society to protect forest and peatland. The JECA
tool assesses whether a jurisdiction has a progressive forest and peat protection agenda, and if
local authorities are committed to the reduction of deforestation and the protection of valuable
ecosystems. Progress on sustainable and socially inclusive intensification through &Green funding
is also monitored throughout the investment period (to ensure continued sustainability of the
Fund), and must adhere to strong social and environmental covenants – in particular, IFC
Performance Standards. Currently, &Green has the following approved jurisdictions: Brazil (State
of Mato Grosso; State of Pará) and country level jurisdictions in: Colombia, Ecuador, Gabon,
Indonesia, Liberia and Peru.19

3.3.3 IFC Performance Standards
The &Green Fund aligns itself with IFC Performance Standards20 identified in the Corporation’s
Sustainability Framework, which is an integral part of IFC’s approach to risk management. All
transactions are assessed against the IFC PS in an extensive due diligence process. Based on this
assessment, a time-bound action plan is established together with the Client to work towards full
compliance with the performance standards in the first years of the loan tenor.
The Policy on Environmental and Social Sustainability describes IFC’s commitments, roles, and
responsibilities related to environmental and social sustainability. The Performance Standards are
directed towards clients, providing guidance on how to identify risks and impacts, and are
designed to help avoid, mitigate, and manage risks and impacts as a way of doing business in a
sustainable way, including stakeholder engagement and disclosure obligations of the client in
relation to project-level activities.
By enforcing these internal standards through its own investment architecture, &Green seeks to
manage environmental and social risks and impacts – within which gender dynamics are embedded
– so that transformational change envisioned by the Fund is sustainable and inclusive.
3.4 IDH Technical Assistance Facility
IDH – the Sustainable Trade Initiative21 was the incorporator of the Stichting &Green Fund. IDH
and &Green work collabouratively and have outlined their joint ambition in a Memorandum of
Understanding. Through its country offices, and through the international sustainable landscapes
programme, IDH works closely with public and private actors, in key jurisdictions for &Green, to
develop potential projects of interest for the Fund, and to support local government in meeting
the Fund’s Jurisdictional Eligibility Criteria.
IDH manages the Technical Assistance Facility (TA Facility) of the Fund. The &Green TA Facility
was formally launched in 2019, and aims to reduce risk and maximise the impact of the &Green
(potential) investment projects, by supporting investment-readiness, monitoring, post-investment
client support and sharing of lessons and knowledge from &Green and its investment projects with
third party stakeholders.
IDH has identified that equitable and meaningful participation of women is key to driving
sustainable intensification and growth in trade, although gender barriers remain rife in commodity
supply chains. To address this concern, IDH has developed a Gender Toolkit, consisting of
practical case examples from IDH and similar projects in congruent sectors, and a Gender
Guide, where opportunities to integrate gender aspects in different programming steps of
projects and inventions are explored. The &Green Fund’s Gender Approach will mobilize
these existing tools.
The role of the TA Facility is to both enhance understanding of gender dynamics in the early
project cycle, and to maximize opportunities for enhanced gender equality and empowerment.
By considering how women and men participate in interventions, the TA Facility strives to enable

3.4.1 IDH Gender Toolkit
The IDH Gender Toolkit22 guides program teams and partners on how to recognize opportunities
related to gender in their programs. Following six programming steps, it provides tools on how to
integrate gender aspects into project design, implementation, and how to develop gender-
responsive indicators for M&E to support gender mainstreaming through the project cycle.
3.4.2 IDH Gender Guide
This guide, part of the IDH Gender Toolkit, presents the six in programming, during which
opportunities arise to integrate gender aspects that may positively influence and leverage greater
impact of a program or interventions. When planning to integrate gender in a successful
investment option, the guide provides entry points for gender analysis or scoping. The &Green
Fund’s Gender Approach builds on the tools and guides developed by IDH. Where appropriate and
necessary, the Fund will mobilise IDH’s TA facility to identify opportunities and barriers that
female and male workers, farmers, and managers face that may influence the success and efficacy
of investment options envisioned through the proposed GCF programme. This will lead to the
implementation of the &Green Fund’s Gender Approach, when sub-projects/investments (Deals)
are identified, should the proposed GCF programme be greenlighted.

Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
4. Programmatic Gender Approach for
the &Green Fund
4.1 Scope
This Gender Approach will provide a framework to accelerate gender mainstreaming investments
through the &Green Fund structure. It informs this Annex 8 and aligns itself with guidance
provided by the GCF on mobilising gender action through climate finance, notably through the
Mainstreaming Toolkit23. The Gender Approach will also influence the overall logical framework
of the proposed GCF programme (in Section E of the GCF Funding Proposal) and identify entry
points for the chosen paradigm shift pathway to have gender and social co-benefits, which will be
identified during the preparation stage.The &Green Fund’s Gender Approach mobilizes IDH’s
existing gender mechanisms, including dispensing gender mainstreaming protocols through the
Technical Assistance Facility, and will utilize IDH’s Gender Toolkit and Gender Guide.
4.2 Two-Tracked Approach
The Green Gender Approach consists of two different tracks: gender-sensitive and gender-
transformative investments:
Gender-sensitive investments acknowledge the different needs and constraints of women and
men without changing the status quo. The client may, for example, realize that the work of female
smallholders in the supply chain is not sufficiently recognized, which limits their access to training.
When providing training to female smallholders, the client could focus on the activities they
perform and attempt to limit the negative effects of a gendered distribution of responsibilities,
such as a heavier workload for women, without challenging the gendered differences themselves.
Gender sensitive approaches can be easily integrated into existing training structures on other
topics since they don’t require underlying gendered behavioral patterns to be addressed.
Gender-transformative investments will address gender imbalances, changing gendered power
relations, and actively building equitable social norms and structures. An organization is aware
that women and men do not have equal opportunities in the household, at community level or at
work. They may, for example, create equal working conditions for women and men, recognizing
that special means may be required to increase the number of women in management positions
and/or to achieve an environment free from gender-based violence (GBV). Gender transformative
approaches are characterized by explicitly centering gender norms and are thus common for
interventions that have the primary goal of addressing gender issues and transforming gender
relations to promote equality.

4.3 &Green Investment Process
These tracks are built in to the investment process of the fund, which consists of several phases:
1) Investment Rationale; in this first phase in the investment process, &Green assesses whether
there is a fit between the prospective investment and &Green’s mission. This is assessed through
a structured Transformational Change assessment. In this assessment, the &Green Fund team will
evaluate whether the prospective investment requires a gender sensitive or a gender
transformative approach. This assessment then triggers different processes in the rest of the
investment process.
2) Deal Note; if the &Green team, including the Investment Committee, agrees that the
prospective investment has a good fit with the Fund’s vision of transformational change, a first
screening will be initiated and presented in a Deal Note. This screening includes a gender-related
screening, and informs the scope of the due diligence process.
3) Credit Application; upon approval of the Deal Note by the Investment Committee and Credit
Committee, a thorough due diligence process is started, using external experts to establish a solid
baseline for the prospective investment, including a gender baseline. With the information
collected in due diligence, a Landscape Protection Plan (LPP) is developed that describes in detail
the impacts of the investment at the landscape level. Attached to this LPP is an Environmental
and Social Action Plan (ESAP) that lists the key milestones and deliverables in a clear, time-bound
format. This also states the targets and the indicators that will be used to measure success. The
LPP and ESAP include the gender outcomes envisioned for the investment. The ESAP and LPP are
strict environmental and social safeguarding covenants that are conditions of the loan contracts
of the &Green Fund. &Green will ensure that clients are onboarded either onto the gender-
sensitive or the gender-transformative pathways. For the former, the client commits to the ‘do-
no-harm’ principle. For the latter, the client has to commit to building capacity to deliver gender-
transformative impact through the proposed investment blueprint.
4) Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV); for each investment, an MRV plan is designed
based on the targets laid out in the LPP/ESAP. &Green implements a robust MRV framework to
assess and report on progress against the various milestones and deliverables, including gender-
related outcomes.
Specifically, the following indicators for social inclusion are measured by the &Green fund. Each
indicators is disaggregated by gender. Note that the KPI framework has recently been revised and
the indicators have not yet been retrofitted to existing portfolio companies. &Green is working to
create a baseline this year to ensure continued monitoring against these indicators going forward.

4.4 &Green Gender Approach
Investment Rationale: At the outset, a gender screening process (IDH – Gender Toolkit – Step 1)
will determine whether the investment will have a gender-sensitive impact or gender-
transformative impact.
Deal Note: In the following stage, whether the investment has been assessed to be gender-
sensitive or gender-transformative, a high-level gender assessment (based on the IDH
methodology) will be conducted. This will involve assessing the client’s fit into the &Green
transformational change narrative, and will be primarily through secondary research
(desktop/online scoping, client’s document screening, and literature review). This assessments
includes a high-level check on SEAH-related risks, derived from the jurisdictional assessments (see
included in this Annex), as well as an assessment of media publications related to SEAH for the
investee and affiliated companies, and an initial check of the policy framework in place to address
SEAH-related risks. Additionally, the country profiles developed for this Assessment (Section 8)
includes available literature on GbV in the different supply chains – and will be a point of departure
for further investigation in the implementation stage.
Due Diligence: In the case of a gender-sensitive project, the high-level gender assessment will
inform the scope of the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) that is a standard
part of &Green’s Environmental & Social due diligence process. The ESIA standardized Terms of
Reference will include a focus on gender risks, including SEAH-related risks, and how to mitigate
these during the investment lifetime. In the case of a gender-transformative investment, in the
due diligence stage, the high-level gender assessment will be used as a background to set up in-
depth gender analysis conducted by technical experts, using the IDH methodology as an entry
point).
Credit Application: In both gender-sensitive and gender-transformative investments, a gender
baseline will be included in the Client’s Landscape Protection Plan (LPP). For gender-
transformative investments, this will include an in-depth analysis of gender barriers of the context
(and chronology) of the investment, which will lead to the development of gender-specific
outputs, outcomes and activities, including SEAH-relation actions. These will be mainstreamed
into the investment’s Environmental and Social Action Plan (ESAP). These targets will be
matched with a realistic timeline, and include a buy-in period, to ensure all stakeholders are
gender-sensitized and are included (to the extent possible) in gender mainstreaming processes, to
ensure both replicability and sustainability.
Deal Approval: After the approval of the credit application, responsibilities of the client relating
to gender mainstreaming (including implementing actions laid out in the ESAP) to remove gender
barriers and improve upon gender baseline at the investment site/through the project will be
codified into the contracts and covenants. Through &Green’s robust monitoring, reporting and
verification (MRV) framework, the gender outputs and outcomes, including SEAH-related outputs,
will be tracked and evaluated (see investment Principles and ESMS Manual section
Monitoring, Reporting and Verification Framework: In this stage, when appropriate, the Fund
will conduct deep dives/case studies into the efficacy of the gender mainstreaming steps taken
through particular deals and lessons learnt/best practices garnered by stakeholders (and the
client) in the process. These studies will complement the Fund’s MRV framework (see Investment

4.4.1 Examples of &Green Gender Approach Applications
Examples of the application of the &Green Gender Approach to the fund portfolio could include
the following:
▪ Affirmative sourcing policies towards women producers: the gender assessment for the 17
countries conducted during the preparation of the programme revealed that women (in most
contexts) are marginalised or side-lined in the different value chains. To ensure that women
get equal benefits from &Green’s supply chain transformation, through improved market
access, better working conditions, bolstered technical assistance and capacity and inclusive
stakeholder engagement, the fund will ensure affirmative sourcing policies towards women
producers.
▪ Training and capacity building to improve gender policies and other conducive factors
within client companies: where capacity is lacking on the operationalisation of gender
equality goals within client companies, &Green can require that the client company conducts
a gender training for their teams, to enable them to implement the gender-related
requirements in the ESAP/LPP.
Revising policies and practices such as improving grievance processes and discussing
harassment during employee gatherings: as part of the IFC PS compliance process (see sub-
section 3.3.3), &Green requires each client company to have a policy framework in place that
promotes gender equality. However, the efficacy of these policies can vary, depending on
cultural, operational and governance factors. Involvement of women – and other marginalised
social groups – in this process has been recognized as critical, and can be a requirement in
the ESAP/LPP. This will be an entry point to engage potential client companies on SEAH, and
to ensure SEAH concerns are mainstreamed as part of company policies and addressed through
grievance processes.
▪ Targeting for equitable representation of women within the company, also at senior
management level: enhanced involvement in decision-making by women supports an inclusive
approach to commodity production. Active promotion of women leadership can accelerate a
company’s journey towards equitable representation, fairer implementational and
commercial policies, as well as improved outcomes, which &Green will promote among client
companies
▪ Proactively training both female and male smallholders on cultivation, processing, and
marketing: through this, &Green will ensure access to training through culturally sensitive
interventions and assist in providing equal access to the extension services provided by clients.
▪ Community awareness and sensitization for generating consensus on &Green principles:
through this step, &Green will introduce an advocacy rubric within its gender approach,
particularly by ensuring that women and men participate in workshops on land tenure and
financial access, including joint management of assets and incomes. This is because building
awareness is communities is critical to ensure gender mainstreaming and social inclusion in a
company’s (future) supply base.

4.4.2 Capacity for Implementation of the &Green Gender Approach
The partners in this facility will draw on both in-house and external expertise for the
implementation of this Gender Approach. This section outlines the various sources of expertise
that are available to the facility, and, where applicable, plans to strengthen this capacity.
The &Green Fund
SAIL Ventures, Investment Advisor to the &Green Fund, has a team of specialists (50% women)
that manages the investment processes. More than one-third of the team is dedicated to
Environmental and Social management, including the implementation of the Gender Approach
across the portfolio. Between the team members, there is a combined experience implementing
a suite of sustainability frameworks across different agricultural sectors globally. This ranges from
certified oil palm, with a focus on gender opportunities for pregnant women in Sierra Leone, to
cotton farming in South Asia, where gender inequality remains a pressing issue.
Michael Schlup, head of Impact & ESG, worked in sustainable cocoa supply chains to implement
sustainability standards for smallholder farmers, impacting women in the sector.
Natalia Pasishnyk, E&S Director, lived and worked in Brazil for 15 years, where she worked to
establish and test the economic and technical feasibility of business models for women cooperatives of
babassu nut breakers in the Brazilian Amazon.
Marthe Tollenaar, also an E&S Director, has been active in the gender space throughout her career,
implementing gender trainings and youth inclusion programs across forestry portfolios in Africa
and Southeast Asia.
The team adopts a flat management structure where we believe that the team as a whole is
responsible for the success of the Fund. Therefore, the SAIL Ventures team will ensure capacity
building on gender-related topics for the whole team. The team is working with IDH to create a
public training that is suited to &Green’s needs, and publicly available to benefit other funds as
well.
IDH – Sustainable Trade Initiative
IDH has established a Global Gender Unit, led by a full-time Senior Manager, to ensure gender
being mainstreamed across all projects. To drive gender organization-wide, IDH has set up an
internal gender champions structure and all IDH staff compulsory must follow a training on gender
equality and all program teams – this includes &Green TAF members – are trained in the use of
the IDH Gender Tool kit. Gender champions, gender Business Units experts and the Global Gender
Unit are available to providing technical support to the program teams to complete the gender
tool and on the interventions design. When needed for specific projects, IDH is also working with
a pool of extern gender experts.
IDH currently is working on making gender/gender tool kit trainings available for external partner
organizations, like &Green. To ensure the applicability of the training to further build gender
capacity in the &Green team, the IDH training has already been reviewed by the &Green ESG team
and feedback will be incorporated in the training that will be made available to &Green.
Client companies
&Green requires that its investee companies have the capacity and the resources to implement
the gender outcomes laid out in the LPP and ESAP. All client companies will have in-house E&S
resources that typically oversee the implementation of ESAP/LPP and facilitate the progress

5.1 Gender in &Green commodity value chains
• Participation of men and women in forestry management is inextricably tied to the
social, cultural, historical, and political contexts of communities where forest
management efforts take place. Gender plays a key role in shaping environmental rights
of control, access, and responsibility that interact with class, race, caste, culture, or
ethnicity to shape ecological change and sustainable livelihoods. (Peach Brown)24
• Women, more so than men – in the &Green target countries – face a number of gendered
and social barriers and constraints when working in agricultural production and
processing. These include: limited equal opportunity to acquire the factors of production
such as land, credit, networks, infrastructure and education; limited time to take
advantage of economic incentives (e.g. by participating in agricultural development
projects) due to women’s existing roles and responsibilities to carry out non-salaried tasks
(e.g. child care, housework), also referred to as the unpaid care economy; discriminatory
gender norms prevalent in communities, markets and institutional structures which favour
male participation and prevent women from having an equal voice in decision-making.
(ProForest)25
• The supply chains that &Green seeks to transform will not only provide improved
economic opportunities for women but can also provide benefits to youth (17 – 25) by
improving livelihoods and skill base in the target countries. Evaluative research on
integrated skill training programmes in Ghana, for example, has revealed that despite
being a leading producer of cocoa and having a burgeoning youth population, it is
estimated that the average age of a cocoa farmer in the country is greater than 50 years.26
The study revealed that to introduce young people to cocoa farming and address the
potential barriers they face in order to do that; a multi-faceted skills training programme
was designed with the ultimate aim of improving and diversifying youth livelihoods. The
training had three key components: i) cocoa academies (which includes agricultural
practices; life skills and financial literacy); ii) business incubators (including
entrepreneurial training, networks, mentoring) and iii) supporting enabling environment
(access to land and finance). These findings reflect the theory of change being proposed
by &Green, and shows the gender-transformative impact the programme can posit to have
on youth in several of the target countries.

• The cattle value chain displays complex gendered factors: some estimate show that women

tasks that are extremely dangerous for women and their reproductive health. Gender-based

• Plantation forests require intensive management, but they grow faster than natural
forests: in 2011, FAO reported that although they accounted only for 5% of the total wood
forest area, it produced 35% of all the world’s wood product. Forestry and forest
management, however, is not gender neutral: socio-cultural and economic reasons,
including land ownership and political underrepresentation, result in women having less
access and control over forest resources and economic opportunities.31 However, women
are powerful agents of forests conservation and management, which &Green recognizes,
as they are in charge with the wellbeing of the household, and tend to adopt a different
approach to forestry than men: less focused on income (timber, mining, mono-cultures)
and more on agroecology, including food security, medicinal plants, and transmission of
invaluable knowledge to future generations. (UN-REDD)32
• This is also the case for soy: In Brazil, one the largest soy producing countries, women
make up 10% of the labour force in the national soy sector, but continue to earn
approximately one quarter less of what men earn and dedicate close to 75% more time to
domestic and care work than men. &Green will ensure that convenants around equal pay
in client companies are in place before finalizing Deal Notes. (ProForest)33
• Strategies for increased participation of women in commercialized and well-developed
supply chains (particularly export-facing ones) require upgrading based on the typology
of the women – as well as the social group they are in - in question. While women in
female headed households may require limited efforts such as tailoring financial products
to their needs or providing interlinked services coupled with prompt payment for their
produce to allow them to produce quality fruits and access lucrative markets, women in
male-headed households need institutionalization of gender-sensitive policies in the
governance of producer groups to enable them to upgrade as value chain integrators and
value chain owners. For gender-transformative investments, &Green will hire external
expertise on gender (if needed) and rely on existing capacities in-house as well as IDH to
assess gender dynamics – as they relate to intersectionalities – and mainstream the findings
into the investment structuring. (CGIAR, 2017)34
• Informal economies and markets are the dominant source of livelihoods in rural areas – and
the engagement in forestry value chains is often crucial for rural women’s livelihoods and
the well-being of their household. (IIED, 2015)35 Women’s use of forest resources tends
to center on low-return products and activities, while men control the production and
commercialization of more profitable forest resources. Women are the main caregivers
of children and ill family members and are responsible for providing food, fuel and fodder.
Given their care work responsibilities of cooking for the household, women’s tree selection
is based on their use and relevance for subsistence. Women prefer trees that provide fruits,
firewood, fodder and increase soil, while men may prefer for commercial species. This
disparity needs to be managed through project design, to ensure benefits of the project

• Women’s time poverty and physical safety concerns limit their access to and use of
forest resources and related activities. Time poverty is used in a very particular sense in
relation to poverty: as working long hours and having no choice to do otherwise. An
individual is time poor if he/she is working long hours and is also monetary poor, or would
fall into monetary poverty if he/she were to reduce his/her working hours below a given
time poverty line. Thus, being time poor results from the combination of two conditions.
First, the individual does not have enough time for rest and leisure once all working hours
(whether spent in the labour market or doing household chores such as cooking, and
fetching water and wood) are accounted for. Second, the individual cannot reduce his/her
working time without either increasing the level of poverty of his/her household (if the
household is already poor) or leading his/her household to fall into monetary poverty due
to the loss in income or consumption associated with the reduction in working time (if the
household is not originally poor). (CIF, 2017)37
• Invisible labour in the value chain needs to be recognized and accounted for: The Food
and Agricultural Organization (FAO) finds that women / vulnerable sections from
marginalized groups are frequently engaged in activities that are undervalued,
including unpaid family labour and work in the men’s fields or in post-harvest tasks for
different value chains. Inclusive project design needs to, therefore, ensure women’s time
burden are not exacerbated by proposed investments, and their participation is not
stymied by existing sociocultural norms, which &Green will aim to assuage through its
Gender Framework.
• Women and members of indigenous communities need to be recognized as important
stakeholders in forest governance, production chains and project design: The
International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) has piloted the Environment and
Gender Index (EGI), which showed that women as well as Indigenous Peoples who rely on
forests are often underrepresented in forest governance at the local, national and
international levels. This is despite women’s key role as primary users of forest resources,
and specific importance in non-timber forest products, in several tropical, forested
landscapes Neglecting women’s role in forest decision-making, therefore, can jeopardize
project outcomes, as women’s specific livelihood needs and preferences can be overlooked
(this is further reiterated through United Nations Programme on Reducing Emissions from
Deforestation and Forest Degradation (UN-REDD)’s evaluations). (IUCN) 38
• Tools and methods related to gender, agriculture, and value chains exist but need to
be reinforced: The Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research (CGIAR)

5.2 SEAH and GbV in the &Green programme
In 1993, the Declaration on the Elimination of Violence against Women (A/RES/48/104) defines
violence against women as “any act of gender-based violence that results in, or is likely to result
in, physical, sexual or psychological harm or suffering to women, including threats of such acts,
coercion or arbitrary deprivation of liberty, whether occurring in public or in private life.”
More recently, as both theoretical and practical work on GbV evolved and became enshrined in
numerous conventions and declarations, article 3 of the Council of Europe’s Convention on
Preventing and Combating Violence Against Women and Domestic Violence (Istanbul Convention)
offered the following definition: “gender-based violence against women shall mean violence that
is directed against a woman because she is a woman or that affects women disproportionately.”
A critical issue identified in this assessment is Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Sexual Harassment
(SEAH)40 – as part of the overall incidence of gender-based violence (GbV) – that is prevalent in
different measures in the commodity supply chains &Green is prioritizing in the target 17
countries. Rooted in structural gender inequality and power imbalances, the prevalence of SEAH
and broader GbV is both caused and exacerbated by exploiting societal gender norms and roles.
These are symptomatic of gender inequality and a tool to reinforce this inequality, including
maintaining or restricting control over natural resources, further entrenching gender inequality in
a cyclical manner.41
Communities and indigenous people in rural areas– where many of the commodity supply chains
will be localised – often face GbV without access to the redress mechanisms that may be
available/or more accessible in urban locations. Many aspects of rural life, including fetching
water and fuel, travelling to remote locations, lack of reliable energy sources, traditional harmful
practices and negative coping mechanisms, all contribute to increase the vulnerability of rural
women and girls, adding to their exposure to the risk of GbV.42 In addition, the potential for
violence related to natural resources is particularly augmented in the face of environmental
stressors and threats. These conditions create situations in which the control over increasingly
scarce or degraded resources is increasingly fraught, resulting in higher tension, increased

negative coping strategies and reduced resilience for families and communities – thus affecting
lives and livelihoods.43
SEAH and GbV, therefore, is widespread in the agribusiness sector. The IFC44 has broken down how
it can be found at all levels of the value chain:
• In farming and primary production: women experience high levels of abuse in the fields.
Asymmetrical power relationships increase the risk of GbV and SEAH. As stated by ILO45,
non-standard forms of work, including temporary work and informal work, are key factors
in creating power differentials for perpetrators to carry out sexual violence and harassment
against women workers. For instance, almost 9 out of 10 horticultural workers in Ethiopia
reported personally experiencing some form of sexual harassment on the farm.46
• In processing and packaging: similarly, GbV and SEAH are common at the processing and
packaging stage, as women are mostly concentrated in low-income, often informal roles,
and are pressured into accepting abuse by their male supervisors in order not to lose their
remuneration
• In logistics and distribution: male drivers transporting agricultural goods over remote
roads and long distances can perpetrate GbV and SEAH. Research in Brazil47 found that one
in five truck drivers admitting to having had sex with a child under the age of 18 while they
were transporting goods.
• At home: domestic violence is widespread at the global level, but the risk is exacerbated
in the agricultural sector. In Europe, women working in agriculture and fisheries have the
highest rates of partner violence of any occupational group: 14% compared with 4% across
all industries.48 Violence in family farms is therefore of particular concern.
&Green recognizes that this is a crucial issue for the implementation of the programme, and
is committed to understanding how SEAH and GBV are entrenched into the overall society and
specifically the selected value chains of the 17 target countries, to be able to address it with
specific actions.

gender considerations. Most importantly, &Green will comply with:
• Performance Standard 2, paragraph 15 on Non-discrimination and Equal opportunity,
therefore committing to take measures to prevent and address harassment, intimidation,
and/or exploitation, especially in regard to women

&Green is aware that GbV and SEAH are global phenomena but that each country has its
specificities, linked with wider conditions of women, gender norms, intersectionalities, and more.
The gender assessments included in this Annex include specific cases of GbV. For instance,
Colombia has high levels of GbV related to the environments, with a streak of attacks against
environmental human rights activists, particularly women, ongoing since the peace agreements
were signed in 2016. On the other hand, in Liberia, the 2019-2020 Demographic and Health Survey
found that 60% of women age 15-49 have experienced physical violence and 9% have experienced
sexual violence. Less than half (42%) of women who have experienced physical or sexual violence
have ever sought help. Rape is one of the most frequently reported crimes in Liberia, and the rate
of sexual violence against women is among the highest in the world.
&Green acknowledges these are starting points that will be used to inform the assessment
phasis of each investment in the implementation countries, so that a full picture of SEAH and
GbV can be drawn and addressed appropriately, both generally and at the level of specific
value chains.
Additionally, IDH has been working extensively on integrating gender in its programmes, and on
reducing GbV specifically. The guiding approach is not merely reputational: by supporting workers
to empower themselves, and by training producers on gender-balanced practices, it is possible to
create safer, happier, and therefore more productive, working environments. By training farming
families on household (financial) decision-making, for example, and the division of roles and
responsibilities in the household, it is possible to promote improvements to the livelihood of the
farmer that also have gender-positive effects.
Two example of this holistic approach include (and that can be both best practices and lessons
learned guide for &Green investments that require IDH technical assistance):
• In the tea sector in Kenya, IDH started work on gender in 2012 through its partnership with
the Ethical Tea Partnership and the Kenya Tea Development Agency, focusing on gender
discrimination and harassment through a social issues program reaching over 1,000
managers, supervisors, and staff members. This led to the following concrete
achievements:
o 50% of women in supervisor positions and 33% of women in management positions;
o More equal employment opportunities – women taking on more roles that were
traditionally reserved for men (e.g. truck driver);
o All factories have sexual harassment and discrimination policies in place; grievance
complaints and disciplinary procedures are included in induction training for new
employees.
• In 2016, IDH convened a platform in Kenya with several tea companies to create a joint
agenda for action to address gender-based violence (GBV) in the sector and share best
practices. IDH will also publish a common training manual on addressing GBV in the Kenyan
tea industry, and is developing a roadmap for plantation management on addressing GBV
alongside field-level projects to implement the roadmap.

6. Gender and socioeconomic baselines for
the target 11 countries
6.1 Composite indices, presented in tables
Gender-transformative climate adaptation and mitigation action requires a thorough and context-
driven gender baseline with appropriate data and indicators. Since this will be a funding facility
and specific projects have not been identified, this study develops a derivative baseline.
Gender assessments will be carried out in the JECA process as needed to add to the country profiles
included in this document, as well as at the investment level. As described in section 3.4, a gender
assessment will be carried out for each investment. This can be an integrated assessment as part
of the ESIA, where we adopt a gender sensitive approach, or a separate more detailed assessment
where we consider a gender transformative approach.
At the outset, composite indices are used as indicative (and not conclusive) measures of current
levels of development and gender equality. As Booysen’s research49 shows, these indices present
challenges as well as advantages. For example, numerous fallacies have been identified in the
methodologies employed in composite indexing. The indices are quantitative, and present
empirical and aggregate measures of complex phenomena – making values apparently objective,
at the cost of subjective nuances. Yet, these also remain invaluable as useful supplements to
income-based development indicators – to understand relative degrees of development. Section 6
presents each index as a table, citing the relevant information for all 11 target countries.
6.2 National aggregate statistics: Poverty, Education,
Labour and Health, presented per country
For these indicators, the data is presented in each country profile to ensure coherence and capture
the full socioeconomic landscape where GCF, FMO and &Green investments may be directed. Each
country profile includes short interpretation of the data, to contextualise the investment
landscape for particular commodities and if applicable, particular regions of the country. For
example, for Brazil (see Section 7), the country profile includes available information on gender
in Mato Grosso and Pará, where the &Green Fund has active JECAs currently. The country profile
also includes brief gender analysis for the priority agro-commodity, such as cattle and soy in Brazil.
The GCF, in its Mainstreaming Gender toolkit for climate change interventions and climate finance
(developed with UN Women), also spotlights the chosen indices as well as the above indicators

Research, (Vol. 59, No. 2). Journal article.

7. Composite Indices
7.1 HDI – UNDP (2019)
The HDI scores presented here is from the 2020 Human Development Report. The Human
Development Index (HDI) is a summary measure of achievements in three key dimensions of human
development: a long and healthy life, access to knowledge and a decent standard of living. The
HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the three dimensions. This technical
note describes the data sources, steps to calculating the HDI, and the methodology used to
estimate missing values.51
The HDI data presented here should be treated as indicative, not conclusive. It provides an
overview of relative degree of development in a particular country but remains a ‘synthetic
indicator’. Recent research has shown the need to supplement the HDI with other indicators
associated with economic and social cohesion, sound development strategies, and sustainability
in growth models.52

7.2 Gender Inequality Index (GII)
The Gender Inequality Index (GII) reflects gender-based disadvantage in three dimensions—
reproductive health, empowerment and the labour market—for as many countries as data of
reasonable quality allow. It shows the loss in potential human development due to inequality
between female and male achievements in these dimensions. It ranges from 0, where women and
men fare equally, to 1, where one gender fares as poorly as possible in all measured dimensions.
GII values are computed using the association-sensitive inequality measure suggested by Seth
(2009), which implies that the index is based on the general mean of general means of different
orders—the first aggregation is by a geometric mean across dimensions; these means, calculated
separately for women and men, are then aggregated using a harmonic mean across genders.
GII, however, should be treated as indicative, not conclusive. Pernmayer finds that the functional
form of the index could be unclear, particularly the inclusion of indicators of relative performance
of women vis-à-vis men, along with absolute women-specific indicators.53

7.3 Gender Development Index (GDI)
The Gender Development Index (GDI) measures gender inequalities in achievement in three basic
dimensions of human development: health, measured by female and male life expectancy at birth;
education, measured by female and male expected years of schooling for children and female and
male mean years of schooling for adults ages 25 years and older; and command over economic
resources, measured by female and male estimated earned income. This further reiterates the
results of the HDI and GII (also by UNDP), and shows the real gender gap in human development
achievements. Geske Dijkstra and Hanmer find that although gender-related development indices
have increased attention towards ‘feminization of poverty and underdevelopment’, more robust

8. Country Profiles
8.1 Brazil
Brazil is widely recognized as a key player in sustaining global food security, with the capacity to
increase production of important agricultural commodities – such as soybean, sugar, cattle, and
coffee – to meet surging international demand. In terms of gender, Brazil has taken concrete
actions to integrate gender equality into the broader policy-making agenda in a participatory
manner and has achieved advances in women’s education and health and equality before the law.
Given that Brazil is a geographically vast and a diverse country, intersections of gender, ethnicity,
and location of residence are associated with systematic welfare disparities across groups, which
has a cascading effect on agro-commodities and value chains.
A key gender barrier in Brazil is limited ownership and lack of control over land exercised by
women and girls.55 The magnitude of the gender asset gap in Brazil, at the national level, is
unknown. This is because agricultural censuses do not adequately cover these issues, despite
consistent advocacy from feminist organizations, such as Espaço Feminista56. Municipal-level
studies57 in Brazil have assessed gender-disaggregation of land ownership and found that only 12%
of total registered land was under women’s names. Moreover, only 5.5% of total agricultural land
was found to be registered under women’s names. This implies, when women own land, their plots
are smaller than men’s plots. From prior available data (2000), the Censo Comunitario Rural, it
was found that only 11% of female respondents were landowners as compared to 89% of male
respondents. Entrenched gender inequality in land ownership can be posited to relate to male
preference in inheritance, male privilege in marriage, and male bias in community.
For the &Green Fund, particularly in the context of priority value chains: cattle and soy, these
issues are relevant. Further, the Fund has two active JECAs in:
Mato Grosso
Mato Grosso58 is Brazil’s third largest state by area and the leading producer of soy, corn, cotton
and cattle. The state is the main grain producer in the country and is expected to contribute with
30% of the national harvest in 2021. In a 2022 study, on federative analysis of gender gaps in
Brazilian states59, using the Global Gender Gap Index methodology (see section 6.4 for GGGI scores
of the target countries), Mato Grosso fared in the bottom quintiles for economic participation and

Pará
Pará63 is Brazil’s second largest state by area and has the ignoble rank of highest deforestation
rates within the country. Pará leads in the production of cassava, açai, pineapple and cocoa
nationally – alongside significant contribution to black pepper, coconut and banana value chains.
Gender studies catering to Pará are limited currently.
8.1.1 Supply chain sectors
Soy
The importance of the soy value chain to Brazil is demonstrated through a variety of data points:
Since 2000, Brazil has doubled its total area of soy plantation to 36 million hectares and is the
reigning largest producer in the world. In Brazil, the 2014 exports of soy products, which include
beans, animal feed and oil, generated a revenue of approximately 30 billion dollars, which was
equivalent to 13% of the total annual export revenue. At the outset of the pandemic, demand for
soy remained high and soybean production in Brazil hit 133 million metric tons in the crop year of
2020/2021.
Demonstrably, soy is a crucial agro-commodity for the 250,000 soy producers in the country (as
estimated by the Associaçao dos Produtores de Soja or APROSOJA in 2017), who are distributed
across 1500 municipalities. Federal, state and municipal governments benefit from soy revenues
through different taxes, and soy is an important contributor to the Brazilian economy.
Socioeconomic research conducted in soy-producing municipalities revealed that soy could be
considered a precursor of socioeconomic development under certain conditions; however, it also
tends to be associated with an increase in income inequality, especially in the agricultural
frontier.64

In Brazil, the soy value chain and the accrual of its benefits are gendered: men and women do not
participate equitably, and women are more likely to do unpaid care work that support men’s
participation (as indicated under SDG 8). Women are underrepresented and make up 10% of the
labour force in the national soy sector – continuing to earn approximately a quarter less of men's
earnings. Women dedicate close to 75% more time to domestic and care work than men.65
Furthermore, less than 15% of all land in Brazil is registered to women and women make up the
majority of the 15 million landless people in Brazil.66
The growth rate of the Brazilian soy value chain in the next decade is expected to continue higher
than the nation’s main competitors, such as the United States and Argentina.67 Therefore, it will
be crucial for programmes like the &Green Fund, to not only delink deforestation from this value
chain, but also to improve gender outcomes: by improving internal operations and by engaging
(and empowering) clients through fund mechanisms and technical assistance to tackle gender
inequality in the soy value chain in Brazil. This will have a gender-transformative outcome by
improving both sustainability and social inclusion in this crucial supply chain for Brazil’s economy
and for global food security.
Cattle
Brazil is the world’s largest beef exporter, exporting approximately one-fifth of its production,
and the sector has a notable environmental footprint, linked to one-fifth of all commodity-driven
deforestation across the tropics.68 Brazil is also the world’s second largest producer of beef, with
2.5 million farmers operating mostly pasture-based production systems where 87 to 90% of cattle
are finished on pasture and approximately 10 to 13% finished in feedlots.69 Although the cattle
value chain has been one of the key drivers of improving local livelihoods and developments, it is
also associated with profound social and environmental challenges.
With some estimates showing that women make up about two-thirds of the 600 million subsistence
livestock keepers worldwide, women’s roles in livestock production and the cattle value chain are
critical. Women’s livelihood activities are and can be influenced by the mutually constructed
intra- and inter-relationships among household members, intermediaries, cooperatives, and
private sector companies. In Brazil, the cattle value chain is traditionally male-dominated and
patriarchal (machista culture), as industrial agribusinesses tend to employ men as skilled

Recently, the cattle (and soy) industry has experienced shifts in gender dynamics: women have
increased their participation. Known as cattle queens, about 31% of farms are now managed and
led by women in the country, according to the Brazilian Agribusinesses’ Association.71 Female
farmers continue to report hurdles as compared to male competitors in accessing training and
credit. High rates of gender-based violence and discrimination are rife in the sector as well.
Therefore, it will be crucial for programmes like the &Green Fund, to not only delink deforestation
from this value chain, but also to improve gender outcomes: there can be, for example, three
pathways through which interventions may influence the livelihoods of women livestock keepers
and their families, according to the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI). This can
include: ensuring affirmative action through inclusion of women producers in the supply chain;
and, securing current and future assets for women by improving their financial and technical
capacities through the programme. Further, the &Green Fund can use its programmatic
investment tools towards sustaining and improving the productivity of agricultural systems while
facilitating greater market access for marginalized gender groups.
8.1.2 Latest Global Gender Gap Index score
Brazil has closed 69.5% of its overall gender gap, achieving a rank of 93rd globally. Only 13.8% of
the Political Empowerment gender gap has been closed to date, ranking Brazil 108th on this
edition’s index, with a 4-rank drop since last year. There are very few women parliamentarians
(15.2%, 17.9% gap closed so far) and ministers (10.5%, 11.7% gap closed so far), and a woman has
been in a head-of-state role for only five years of the last 50 (12% gap closed so far).
Brazil’s GGGI score in 2021 was 0.695, which means it ranks 25th at the regional level and 93rd
globally. Sub-scores are as follows:

• Income inequality is gendered and racialized in Brazil: Poverty in Brazil is driven by
extreme inequalities in income, which has many facets. While there is stratification of
income groups, within these, women, particularly Afro-Brazilian women, experience
gendered and racialized wage gaps. In 1981, women were paid 55.7% of men’s wages,
which has steadily climbed up to 71% in 2010, according to the World Bank.
• Female-headed households in rural settings continue to face poverty: Data analysis from
2009 reveals that female-headed households account for roughly 27% of poor rural people
in Brazil, against 13% in 1970.82 This spike can be termed the feminization of rural poverty:
which may be caused by male outmigration, or because women may be single parents,
while having to manage family farms as well as their household.

Given the breadth of the Brazilian economy and geography, the labour market exhibits complex
dynamics. The World Bank finds that the over-all gender gap in labour force participation and
employment has not changed substantially over the last decade, but there are important
differences in participation rates and employment situation across geographic areas. By region,
for example, labour force participation rates for women are highest in the South (60.7 percent)
and lowest in the Northeast (53.7 percent). In 2008, a CEPAL (Comisión Económica para America
Latina y el Caribe) review found that discrimination against gender wage gap in Brazil is wide –
and is linked to worsened poverty in the country. Additionally, the gender wage gap is racialized
– Afro-Brazilian women are consistently discriminated through lowest pay for the same work.
• Linkage of household wealth and women’s income: Women’s lower incomes impacts the
performance of socioeconomic indicators at the household level, while introducing limits to
decision-making and power within these contexts. For example, women make up 10% of the
labour force in the national soy sector of Brazil – but continue to earn approximately a
quarter less than men's earnings, and dedicate close to 75% more time to domestic and care
work than men.
• Unpaid care work and invisible work: The sexual division of labour is also reflected in
differences between men and women in the number of hours worked in paid work and
domestic tasks. In Brazil, women tend to spend an average of 22.7 hours per week on
domestic work, which is four times as much as that reported by men (~5.5 hours per week).
In a time use study, the World Bank pegged unpaid care work at 11.6% of total time use for
women as compared to 5.1% that men reportedly spend. This gendered division drives down
women’s earnings by limiting the time they spend on paid activities, and (often) by leading
women to seek employment that has flexible or shorter hours (which, in turn, is likely to be
found in the informal sector or in low-growth entrepreneurship). Further, employment of
women in agriculture is ostensibly lower than men (4.02% as compared to 12.8%), IFAD
finds107, in tandem with the fact that rural women’s labour is often invisible. Therefore,
women’s contributions to their households – in terms of both housework and raising children
as well as their work in agriculture and other economic sectors – are immense, but often
invisibilised and not remunerated.

invisible-visible

8.2 Cameroon
Cameroon is a major exporter of several agricultural commodities. which account for 34% of its
total exports including cocoa beans, sawn wood, rubber, palm oil, tobacco, cotton, bananas,
maize and cassava. The primary sector contributes to approximately 17.4% of the country’s GDP
and employs close to 43% of the country’s active population.108 For the &Green Fund, palm oil,
rubber and plantation forests are priority value chains in Cameroon, where the fund aims at
establishing a JECA agreement.
According to the National Gender Policy Document 2011-2020 by the Ministry of Women's
Empowerment and Family (Ministère de la Promotion de la Femme et de la Famille: MINPROFF),
regional, ethnic and religious factors dominate and introduce variations in the gender status quo
in Cameroon. There is, however, a persistent value of gender division of labour in which men take
the productive and public roles and women take reproductive and domestic roles.109 In Cameroon,
women’s labour force participation rate is high and they contribute to household income.110
However, women’s work tends to be undervalued as it is perceived as supplementing income of
the husband/male head of the family, regardless of actual content of the task or income.111 Land
and tenure rights also remain a challenge – despite the role women play in ensuring national food
security in the country.112 This is an important factor to consider, when mainstreaming gender
into established commodity supply chains in the country.113
The &Green Fund will address women’s specific challenges in palm oil, rubber and plantation
forestry sector, including access to land, access to finance and to labour and non-labour
inputs, to ensure smallholder women farmers can contribute to and benefit from sustainable
intensification within these supply chains through its investment thesis.
8.2.1 Supply chain sectors
Palm oil
Cameroon is the largest producer of palm oil in Central Africa yielding over 450,000 tons in 2020
with over 170,000 ha of land dedicated to this activity. The expansion of production in recent
years has accelerated deforestation with a recent study showing that 67% of oil palm expansion
from 2000-2015 occurred at the expense of the forest in Southwest Cameroon. While Cameroon is
a significant producer of palm oil, producing more than 2.6 million tonnes in 2020, it cannot keep

CIFOR finds that women workers’ contributions to large and smallholder oil palm production are
either less visible, rendering them as shadow workers, or women are overrepresented in the
‘casual worker’ category, with limited entitlement to decent working conditions.114 Traditional
palm oil processing have given way to industrial, foreign direct investment-led palm plantations –
which have reified exploitative socioeconomic structures and have not led to targeted
empowerment of women.
The expansion of industrial plantations, such as palm oil in Cameroon, require large areas of land,
which consequently diminishes the ecosystem goods and services that local communities— and in
particular, women — previously used and often, subsisted on.115 Women living in and around agro-
industrial plantations in Cameroon are also exposed to increased levels of gender-based violence: they
have suffered physical and psychological violence, mainly when seeking their livelihoods — which have
become scarce due to the presence of these industries.
Rubber
Rubber exports account for around USD 38 million of Cameroonian exports (USD 28 million from
natural dry rubber and USD 10 million from natural rubber). The main private agro-industrial
entities contributing to Cameroon’s rubber production are Hevecam (54,000 ha) and Sudcam
(45,000 ha), both owned by Halcyon Agri. Taking together, these represent the largest rubber
plantation in the world.
Major exports destinations are Europe and the U.S – and as production has expanded in recent
years, so too has deforestation to clear the way for new plantations. In 2021, the national
government started a programme aiming to develop palm oil and rubber tree plantations in the
country by providing support to small farmers and restoring and redeveloping existing plantations
to boost yields per hectare. This programme is expected to yield an additional 6,667 tonnes in
2022 and bolster farmers’ revenues.
Although specific case studies/reports on rubber and gender dynamics in Cameroon are not
currently available, the evidence on women’s participation and eventual benefits depending on
diverse factors including: intra-household power dynamics, cultural norms, laws, policies and
regulations – has been mounting.116 The differences in gender roles/responsibilities of men and
women coupled with the power relations in terms of access to and control over resources, pose a
major challenge for Cameroonian women in the production of and benefits from cocoa, palm oil,
rubber and timber.

Plantation forestry
Cameroon has about 22 million hectares of dense rainforests, i.e. 46.25% of the national
territory.117 With this potential, Cameroon is one of the four main countries with forests in the
Congo Basin. However, mining, agro-industries and other supply chains have affected extensive
damage on these ecosystems, resulting in deforestation and degradation of forests. The Ministry
of Forestry and Wildlife (Ministère des Forets et de la Faune: MINFOF) recognizes that – to stem
the above predicament – there is a crucial need for more innovative measures that will likely
enable plantation forests to effectively play their role of increasing production per unit area, and
delinking deforestation from supply chains important for the Cameroonian economy. For example,
the two main forestry exports in Cameroon are sawn wood and rough wood. In 2020, Cameroon
exported USD 400 million in sawn wood, mainly going to China (USD 76 million, Belgium (USD 61
million) and Viet Nam (USD 56 million).118 To that effect, the National Plantation Forests
Development Programme 2020 – 2045 has been designed and is currently in implementation.119
Research conducted by Perez et al. (2002) presents a gender analysis of forest product markets in
the Humid Forest Zone of Cameroon, which demonstrate that communities benefit from a range of
non-timber forest products as well. The study describes the functioning of the market and analyzing
male-female differences and confirmed that gender is the main basis for differentiating size of business,
product specialization, and market strategies among traders.120 Priorities to improve trade also show
some male-female differences.121 At the same time, there are no consistent differences in profit
margins between genders, indicating that trading efficiency is similar, and that, given the right
conditions, women entrepreneurs can be as successful as men. The results also indicate that the gender
gap could be closing among the younger generation entering the market – which is an important
dividend for improving supply chains in the country.
8.2.2 Latest Global Gender Gap Index score
Cameroon has closed 69.2% of its overall gender gap, achieving a rank of 96th globally. Only 20.2%
of the Political Empowerment gender gap has been closed to date, ranking Cameroon 74th on this
edition’s index, with a slight improvement since last year’s classification. While women
parliamentarians represent 33.9% of parliamentarians (51.3% of the gap closed), there are only
14.9% of women in ministerial positions (17.5% of the gap closed) and no woman has been in a
head-of-state role in the last 50 years.

A World Bank study on Cameroon’s health care system shows that public spending on health in
Cameroon is low (1.5% of GDP) which is below the average for countries in sub-Saharan Africa.139
As a result, many of the health care costs are borne by households out-of-pocket with high regional
disparities in terms of public investment in health, health insurance coverage and health staff
distribution. These regional disparities broadly reflect the poverty profile of the country and have
distinct effects on the health of women:
• Gender-based violence is widespread with an estimated 34% of Cameroonian women
between the ages of 15 and 49 having experienced physical violence while 21% have
experienced sexual and physical violence.140
• Maternal mortality ratios remain high in Cameroon at 529 deaths for 100,000 live births,
which is above the 20 which the WHO uses as a threshold. There are also important
differences with the North of the country hosting several displaced populations (who
usually have worse maternal health). A study finds that in the North, ‘any level of
education and being Muslim were protective against maternal mortality’ while ‘domestic
violence and ethnicity were associated with maternal death in the South’ (increasing age
and education also decreased maternal mortality in the South).141
• Under-five mortality is largely driven by diseases such as malaria, pneumonia and
diarrhoea.142

Cameroon spent 14.4% of its total government expenditures on education in 2020147 with progress
occurring regarding decreasing illiteracy over the last decade. Despite these changes, an
education gender gap persists with women and girls encountering numerous challenges along their
education pathway:
• Gross enrolment rates are highly gender-differentiated with 80% of girls between 6 and 14
attending schools against 94% of boys.148 This can be attributed to a number of factors
including poverty, which leads to women leaving school earlier in order to join the labour
force, high rates of youth pregnancy and child marriage as well as traditional values which
generally lead parents to first un-enrol girls as opposed to boys.149 Poverty and lack of
schooling are intimately linked with data by UNFPA showing that 71% of child bribes come
from poor households while UNICEF shows that 31% of teenage girls are married before the
age of 18.150
• Gaps in enrolment rates between the genders are still large for secondary education (64.6%
for boys versus 55.4% for girls in 2016) but decrease when looking at tertiary education
(15.1% for men versus 13.4% for women).151

Access to employment particularly in the formal sector whether public or private remains
challenging for Cameroonian women:
• In 2010-2011, the informal sector represented approximately 90% of jobs followed by the
public sector (5.8%) and private formal sector (3.7%).162 Women tend to be overrepresented
in the informal sector (93.8% against 87.5% for men) particularly in the agricultural sector
where wages and crop yields are lower.
• Men’s wages are between 1.5 and 2 times higher than those of women. Gender wage gaps
are less pronounced in the formal sector than in the informal sector.163 However, women
tend to be under-represented in the formal private sector where there are twice as many
men as women that are employed.164 In the public sector, another source of formal
employment, there were only 11.6% of women in 2012.165
• Unemployment as a percentage of the labour force is also higher for women (4.5%)166 than
for men (3.3%).167
• Results from a 2014 survey show that women spend 212 minutes a day on unpaid care work
as opposed to 74 minutes for men with a large portion of this spent on unpaid domestic
services for their own final use within the household.168

8.3 Colombia
Colombia has the third largest economy in Latin America, and 80% of its 50 million inhabitants
live in urban areas. In addition to deep-rooted social, economic and gender disparities, Colombia
is currently the most unequal country in Latin America in terms of land distribution: 1% of
landowners possess 80% of the territory.169 Colombia has high levels of gender-based violence in
relation to the environment: particularly, a track record of attacks against and murders of
environmental human rights defenders, particularly women, which continues to increase since the
peace agreement was signed in 2016.170
Women defenders are socially active in the country, and they often tend to be small farmers,
indigenous or Afro-Colombian. They are concentrated in rural areas where households are under
the poverty line, affected by the long conflict that has lasted for more than five decades. Gender
identities in Colombia are intersectional – which is an important factor to consider during gender
assessments at localised programme and investment sites.171
It is estimated that 70% of the food eaten in the country is produced by small farmers, who can
play a key role in the food security and climate adaptation as well as mitigation efforts of the
country.172 Key value chains include plantain, banana, rice, maize, cattle, coffee, cocoa, palm oil
and plantation forestry. For the &Green Fund, cattle, coffee, cocoa, palm oil and forestry are
priority value chains in the country, where the Fund has an active JECA.
8.3.1 Supply chain sectors
Cattle
Colombia’s cattle sector is very broad, with a cattle inventory of approximately 28 million heads,
distributed across 623,792 farms173, the fourth largest herd in Latin America. In 2017, livestock
raising contributed to 1.4% of the country’s GNP, generating 6% of national employment and 19%
of agricultural employment.174 In 2014, Colombia reported having 34M ha2 of pasture, of which
27.9% were classified as unmanaged.175 While the sector holds a great economic value, studies
suggest that expansion of cattle represents one of the biggest drivers of deforestation in the
