country:176 in 2019, approximately 89% of the total farmland was devoted to cattle (on average,
0.7 head of cattle per hectare177). Cattle (as well as palm oil and illicit cultivations, such as coca)
is also tightly linked with the land grabbing phenomenon, as reported by a recent investigation
led by WWF and InSight Crime, funded by USAID.178 According to the Colombia’s Institute of
Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM), in the Northern departments of
Guaviare, Caquetá and Meta, up to 64,000 hectares have been destroyed between January and
March 2020, an 80% increase compared with the same period in 2019.179 Moreover, Tapasco et al.
(2019) note that the livestock sector produced 26% of Colombia’s total GHG emissions, with cattle
amounting to 95% of the sector’s emissions.180
There is also a key gender dimension to the cattle and livestock sector in Colombia: there seems
to be a general gendered pattern of labour allocation in the country, due to which men are
responsible for farm and livestock activities, and women are assigned to household and care
work.181 A study conducted in the livestock intensive region of Cauca, in fact, found that only 13%
of women reported livestock as their principal activity, indicating care work as their principal
occupation instead. About 70% of them, indicated some kind of agricultural activity as their
secondary occupation, 43% of which is livestock rearing.182 The study analyses the effect of
extreme weather events on livestock production, focusing on the prolonged drought that hit the
Cauca region in 2015-2016.
The impact on labour allocation was not gender neutral, with 80% of men reporting a negative
trade-off between work and leisure time, against 60% of women reporting a negative trade-off
between housework and farm work, therefore juggling between different responsibilities.
However, sustainable livestock programmes, such as the World Bank-supported Mainstreaming
Sustainable Cattle Ranching project, have shown promising results of how the silvopastural
approach can advance rights and wellbeing of small farmers, including women and internally
displaced people, while also improving the sustainability of cattle practices.183
It is, therefore, essential that investment and reforestation programmes engaged in this value
chain, such as the &Green Fund, consider the gender disparities that affect the sector. This
includes addressing the significant disparity in terms of time poverty, and by enhancing awareness
and equal access to technical knowledge of sustainable cattle practices, to improve environmental
as well as gender outcomes.

Palm oil
Colombia is the largest producer of palm oil in Latin America, as well as the fourth largest184 and
fastest185 growing producer in the world. According to the National Federation of Oil Palm Growers
of Colombia (FEDEPALMA), palm oil is the fourth largest export in the agricultural sector and
created 177,400 jobs186 in 2019. These data points underscore the importance of this value chain
for the Colombia economy.
The palm oil value chain is, apparently, less responsible for deforestation in Colombia as in other
countries (notably, Indonesia and Malaysia): according to the Colombia’s Institute of Hydrology,
Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM), only 0.25% of deforestation between 2011 and
2017 is related to palm oil production, and overall share of certified palm oil increased from 5%
in 2014 to 20% in 2018.187 Moreover, after a complex tripartite labour deal supported by ILO188,
there has been a significant improvement in labour condition, wages and job formalization in the
sector.
However, palm oil companies have been accused water and air contamination189, with severe
negative effects on the health of nearby communities. Contamination has a significant, negative
cascading effect on women, generally tasked with collection of water and household care,
increasing their workload.
In addition, women are generally discriminated against in the palm oil sector at the global level:
they have fewer or no opportunities on and around plantations compared with men, they usually
work in lower status and lower paid positions, and are much more likely to be employed informally,
limiting their access to social security and basic services. The limited, informal status of women
in the sector also causes them to undertake dangerous tasks with little or no protection, exposing
them to risks and harm.190
Considering these factors, the &Green Fund will activate solutions to address these disparities and
gaps, to increase social inclusion in the palm oil value chain. This wil ensure that current inequality
is not further exacerbated, and, in fact, will be combated to advance the human rights of all
workers and communities involved in the palm oil value chain. In particular, clients of the Fund

Coffee
Colombia is the third largest coffee producer in the world, behind Brazil and Viet Nam. Around
86% of the coffee is exported as green coffee, while the remaining product is roasted and
consumed locally. Colombia is also an important producer of certified coffees, with 7 certification
programmes, among which Colombia is the second-largest producer of Rainforest Alliance-
certified coffee and the largest producer of Fairtrade-certified coffee.191 While coffee is a key
value chain for the Colombian economy, it has been facing increasing climatic and economic
challenges: between 2017 and 2019, Colombia lost nearly 100,000 acres of coffee plantations
(more than 4% of the land under coffee cultivation), according to the Colombia’s National
Federation of Coffee Growers. The decreasing sunlight time, extreme weather events and spread
of fungal diseases and insects have hit the sector. Out of approximately 500,000 farms, 95% are
smaller than 12 acres.192
A study conducted on gender relations in the coffee value chain highlights strong perception of
gender roles, with ingrained conceptions about femininity and masculinity, identified by
respondents as sound reasoning to assign “lighter” tasks to women and to justify “belonging” of
women to the home realm.193 These perceptions of gender roles influence the tasks that women
carry out in coffee production. Such tasks tend to include those relegated to the household space,
so they can simultaneously do care work and farm work (drying, processing, vegetable garden,
preparation of meals for workers, small livestock breeding. Other tasks include: coffee bean
selection; record-keeping, with the perception of women being more organized and having more
time.
In other words, the roles in the farm mirror the roles in the household as well as within the
community. It is also reported that, while the farm is considered family property, the formal
owner is almost exclusively a man, unless the women received inheritance or were specifically
assigned a plot. This is an active discriminatory practice, which also affects the possibility of
women to access resources and income generated by the production, as well as their involvement
in decision-making. As a result of these practices, women are also less involved in technical and
training activities and opportunities.194
However, there is evidence that women-centred projects linked with coffee production (such as
the positive case of the Asociacion de Mujeres Cafeteras del Occidente del Huila, or the
Association of Rural Women Almaguereñas, supported by UN Women) have a positive impact on

Cocoa
While cocoa has long been cultivated and consumed domestically, Colombia is the 10th largest producer
globally, with just 1% market share.196 In 2020, there were 52,000 producer families, 11,148 tons exported
and 63,416 produced, with 165,000 jobs created.197
In 2018 Colombia signed up for the Cocoa and Forest Initiative, with the commitment of ending deforestation
in the cacao supply chain by 2020. A recent baseline study198 conducted by the International Centre for
Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) found that cocoa cultivation is not linked with deforestation, but that its
production is, in many cases, associated with areas affected by conflict and presence of illegal crops, which
also happen to be areas with high rate of deforestation. Cocoa could be an agent of forest conservation, as
well as driving peace as an alternative income from illicit cultivations. However, most cocoa farms in
Colombia have low productivity and are smaller than needed to produce sufficient income: the value chain
needs to be developed and made profitable in order to exploit its environmental and social benefits.199
As in all the other value chains analysed, the strong perception of gender roles defines the
participation of women in the cocoa sector. The association of women and reproductive work
excludes them from productive and community spaces200, causing an imbalance: participation in
the productive space is only 22% for women, compared to 58.6% for men, while men participation
in the reproductive space is only 6%, compared with 86.3% for women. Community space seems
to be less imbalanced, with an almost equal representation, which might be a way to reduce
gender gaps. The role of women in the cocoa sector has proven to be essential for advancing
sustainability, as:
▪ they consistently and creatively adopt technical recommendations to improve crop productivity
and sustainability;
▪ they pass on the knowledge acquired in training sessions on the technical, environmental and
social aspects of cultivation to their families and the wider community; and,

reduce the gender gaps at the same time.
Plantation forestry
A study conducted by IDEAM in 2017202 found that almost 50% of all timber produced in Colombia
is illegally sourced. Colombia holds the potential to plant 24 million hectares of forests, against
the 511,000 that have currently been planted203: there is therefore considerable growth potential
in this area. In 2008, Colombia was the first Latin American country to introduce an Intersectoral
Pact for Legal Timber (PIML), which was supported by FAO-EU Forest Law Enforcement,
Governance and Trade (FLEGT) programme and involved the Colombian Ministry for Environment
(MADS), communities, producers, civil society and law enforcement agencies. It now includes 70
public and private sector organizations, and has become a model for sustainable forestry in the
region.
Plantation forests require intensive management, but they grow faster than natural forests: in
2011 FAO reported that although they accounted only for 5% of the total wood forest area, it
produced 35% of all the world’s wood product.204 Forestry and forest management, however, is
not gender neutral: socio-cultural and economic reasons, including land ownership and political
underrepresentation, result in women having less access and control over forest resources and
economic opportunities.205 However, women are powerful agents of forests conservation and
management, as they are in charge with the wellbeing of the household, and tend to adopt a
different approach to forestry than men: less focused on income (timber, mining, mono-cultures)
and more on agroecology, including food security, medicinal plants, and transmission of invaluable
knowledge to future generations.206
The &Green Fund will therefore mainstream gender into the forestry value chain, maximising the
impact women can have on conservation and sustainable exploitation of plantation forests, as well
as advancing their participation to decision-making, access to resources and efforts for land
ownership.

The World Bank213 finds that monetary poverty increased in Colombia from 34.7% in 2018 to 35.7%
in 2019, with an additional 662,000 thousand people falling into poverty. Inequality continued to
increase, as the GINI index214 reached 52.7 in 2019: among the highest in Latin America.
• Colombia is one of the most unequal countries in the world, with a GINI Index of 52.7 and
inequality increasing both in urban and rural areas.
• Income inequality is historically very high in Colombia. According to the World Bank, in
2017, 10% of the population received 39% of the total income. In 2019 Households in the
bottom 40 percent of Colombia's income distribution experienced little income growth, yet
still positive compared to the reduction in average income per capita growth. In rural
areas, while the economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic were less devastating than in
urban centres, female poverty remains higher: 49.4% compared with 44.6%.
• Income inequality causes significant social and economic hurdles, and it can impede
upward social mobility by diminishing opportunities for marginalized groups, including
women, the poor, indigenous groups and children.215 It is important to remember how in
the case of Colombia, as indicated at the beginning, intersectionalities can aggravate
inequality. While Colombia has made progress in advancing women’s rights in the last
decade, the gender gap in employment remains a challenge, with higher unemployment
rates and a significant wage gap.216
• Female-headed households have historically experienced increased levels of poverty
compared to male-headed households, especially in rural areas.217 The situation has been
aggravated by the pandemic: poverty in FHH was 38.2% in 2019, and it rose to 46.7% in
2020. In comparison, in the same period, poverty among male-headed households
increased by 5.7%.218

Colombia has made significant progress in the field of education, as observed by the World Bank:
the literacy gender gap has been negligible in the last two decades, and women now outnumber

Colombia invests a share of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on education which is in line with

the education sector in Colombia, as identified by the report:
• In Colombia, the proportion of children from the bottom quartile of the PISA index of

Colombia adopted a healthcare system based on universality in 1993.233 Since then, citizens are
obliged to join one of two possible insurance schemes: a contributory plan for employees and self-
employed workers with contributory capacity or a subsidized (non-contributory) scheme for
informal workers and low-income self-employed workers. Members of the two schemes are
entitled to the same benefits, with a single service package available. The system had a positive
impact on access to healthcare for rural and poor communities and since its adoption, maternal
and neonatal mortality rate has fallen by 40%. However, there are significant challenges and risk
for women and girls in Colombia:
• Maternal mortality rates or MMRs: MMRs in Colombia has declined in the last decades, but
at 65.48 remains much higher than the acceptable rate of twenty maternal deaths per
100,000 live births that the WHO deems acceptable. In addition, economic inequality has

Colombian labour market was hit harshly by the pandemic, and its effect were felt in particular
in the urban centres, where is concentrated 80% of the overall country population. While some of
the damages were absorbed and the economy adjusted in 2021, the country has not yet returned
to the pre-pandemic employment levels.249 Employment remains gendered and women are both
burdened by unpaid care work and discriminated in terms of wage, social security, formalization
of labour and access to training:
• Women’s unemployment has historically been higher in Colombia, and women were
particularly affected by the pandemic shock to the labour market: in March 2022,
unemployment rate was 16.5% for women, compared with 10.3% for men.250
• The World Bank251 finds that civil status, children, education and economic background are
all factors determining women participation in the labour market: women who were in a
union (divorced, widowed or separated) are most likely to be working (75.6% of all women
workers), followed by women in a union (57.8%) and by single women (38.5%). Women
without children are found to be working less frequently, but among mothers participation
decreases with number of children. Women who have completed tertiary or primary
education are much more likely to find work than women who complete the secondary cycle
(44%) who are even less likely to work than those with no education at all (49%). Women
from the highest income quintile (61.2%) are also found to be working more frequently than
those from the lowest quintile (39.1%).
• According to the National Survey on Time Use252, women spent on average 7 hours and 46
minutes to unpaid work, compared with 3 hours and 6 minutes for men. The World Bank, in
2017, estimated women dedicate approximately 5% of their time to unpaid care work,
compared with 2.9% for men. IN 2017, It was estimated that unpaid care work amounted to
as much as 20% of GDP. As indicated above, the conflict and added burden of unpaid care
work influences the level of participation to work and community life, access to economic

8.4 Côte d’Ivoire
Côte d'Ivoire is the world’s largest producer and exporter of cocoa (30% of the world production),
one of the three bigger producer and exporter of cashew, and a major exporter of palm oil, coffee
and oil. The country’s economy is mainly based on agriculture. The primary sector contributes
USD 13.12 billion to GDP, or 21.4%, and employs 40% of the country's active population. For the
&Green Fund, oil palm and cocoa are priority value chains in Cote d’Ivoire, where the fund
aims at establishing a JECA agreement.
8.4.1 Supply chain sectors
Palm Oil
Côte d’Ivoire is West Africa’s second-largest palm oil producer after Nigeria and eighth largest
overall. After annual production fell from 415,900 tonnes in 2010 to 360,000 in 2012, the country
has successfully stabilised its annual production at around 400,000 tonnes per year, with local
news reporting that the industry is worth CFA550bn (€825m) and affects upwards of 2m Ivorians.
The government intends to further boost this industry, largely dominated by small village
plantations responsible for up to 60% of the country’s production, through the National Agricultural
Investment Programme (Programme National d’Investissement Agricole, PNIA). Launched in 2016
for the 2016-20 period, the PNIA aims to increase production from around 400,000 tonnes per year
to 600,000 tonnes.
As the fourth-highest income generator in the Ivorian economy, the palm oil industry is poised for
growth over the next few years, thanks in large part to the government’s 2016-20 PNIA. Home to
Africa’s largest palm oil refinery, Côte d’Ivoire’s palm oil industry is primarily driven by small
producers located in villages as opposed to Indonesia or Malaysia, where large-scale industrial
plantations are common. Through investments from the government, Côte d’Ivoire’s palm oil
industry will be able to significantly expand production and continue exporting to neighbouring
countries, a market very much in demand given oilseed shortages.
Approximately 85% of palm oil plantations are between one to five hectares, highlighting the
importance of smallholders in this subsector.254 Around 60% of Côte d’ Ivoire’s palm oil comes from
small village plantations. Ranging in size from 3-5 ha, small plantations are a strong source of
sustainable employment for Ivorians. The remaining 40% of production is handled by large-scale
industrial groups, which are able to produce almost double the tonnage per ha than small
producers. Such industrial groups include Dekeoil and SIFCA. SIFCA is one of the largest producers
of palm oil in West Africa. Its local subsidiary, PALMCI, holds 39,000 ha of land for industrial palm
oil production and oversees and supports another 27,000 cultivators across 133,000 ha of small
village plantations, enabling it to account for the production of up to 300,000 tonnes of palm oil
per year.
Palm oil is a key commodity for women in Cote d’Ivoire: traditionally, it is them who manually
produce it, with some growers selling part of their produce to artisanal women processors.255 A

Scenarios, p. 37

recent study256 found that the productivity gender gap related to export crops, including palm oil,
has reduced significantly between 2008 and 2016, to the point of being nearly closed. While this
gain is partly driven by specific efforts by the Government to include women in agricultural
production, and is evident in the high use of non-labour inputs (pesticide and fertilizers) used by
female-headed households, the gender gap reduced also due to lower landholdings by female
headed households. Women are also exponentially less likely to access export crops and face
challenges in land tenure: the 2015/1016 census showed that only 8% of women hold a land title,
compared with 22% of men. Moreover, while widows’ right to inherit land is protected by law,
actual inheritance practice varies geographically.257
Cocoa
As the world’s largest cocoa grower, Côte d'Ivoire relies heavily on the commodity as a key
economic export and major contributor to GDP. In 2020, cocoa accounted for nearly USD 4 billion
export revenue. Recent research from UNEP found that the introduction and expansion of
agroforestry throughout Côte d'Ivoire could help increase forest cover and reach the goal of
doubling it to 20% by 2030.258 Moreover, the World Cocoa Foundation found that agroforestry
measures such as introduction or increase of forest trees on 1.8 million hectares of low shade
cocoa could meet the agroforestry definition of 30% shade, well exceeding the national goal of
one million hectares across cocoa, oil palm and rubber combined.259
The cocoa value chain is gendered in Cote d’Ivoire: an assessment led by Fair Labour Association
on women’s role in Nestle’s cocoa supply chain260 found that women face a number of risks and
challenges. Women have a crucial role throughout the production chain, from field creation up to
the drying process, which goes largely unrecognised in the Ivorian society. In fact, women have
considerably less access to land, labour and non-labour inputs, education and capital. Women are
also undercompensated, lack adequate access to representation and collective bargain, as well as
to proper health and safety equipment. This is compounded by risks posed to health by hard
physical work (which in the case of women is exacerbated by their double burden of unpaid care
work: most women interviewed reported working on average 16 hours a day) and insufficient
access to quality basic services in rural areas. Women in cocoa-producing household have a high
illiteracy rate (60%), and that, plus traditional gender norms identifying the woman as inferior to
her husband, does not contribute to women’s access to technical and educational opportunities,
as well as to decision-making processes.
The &Green Fund will take these barriers and challenges into account, to fully acknowledge
women’s role in the cocoa supply chain, supporting efforts to increase access to land, training and
inputs, supporting a safe and equal division of labour. Community-based initiatives to raise
awareness of women’s rights, equal decision-making and fair participation will also be explored.

Cote d’Ivoire has experienced sustained economic growth in the last decade, which has been
linked to considerable poverty and inequality reduction. Poverty (at national poverty level) went
from 44.4 in 2015 to 39.5 in 2018. Similarly, inequality has also decreased, with the Gini Index268
going from 41.5 in 2015 to 37.2 in 2018. However, as reported by the World Bank, GDP growth is

and non-agriculture self-employed occupations, mostly taken by women with no formal
occupation.269
• In 2013, the World Bank reported270 official statistics data which indicated 75% of rural

land, education and basic services, as well as the application of traditional gender norms
and roles, all contribute to prevent women from escaping poverty.

Cote d’Ivoire has invested in education, and has witnessed improved outcomes in the last decade.
However, the education gender gap persists, and women and girls encounter numerous challenges
in their educational pathway:
• According to official government data, while progress has been made since 2011, data in
2018 still showed a considerable gap in terms of enrolment and completion throughout the
school cycles, and with particular emphasis on secondary education. The completion rate
for girls in primary education in 2018 was 82.2%, compared with only 34.6% for the first
cycle of secondary school, where girls represent 44% of students, for a gender parity gap
of 0.86.280
• Quality of education is also a key concern, and tightly linked with poor performance: in
2021 the achievement rate of girls at the primary cycle exam (CEPE) was 53.13%, whereas
at the Junior Secondary School Certificate (BEPC) it was 41.25%. In the same year, only
29.61% of girls managed to obtain their Baccalaureat certificate (high school diploma).281
• While access to education for girls increases, the choice of educational and career paths is
still skewed towards jobs and topics that are perceived “feminine”. According to UNESCO,
only 16% female students in Cote d’Ivoire are enrolled in STEM faculties, and boys perform
better than girls in math both in early and in late primary.282 Financial literacy is also a key
obstacle: 46% of women are numerate, compared with 62% of men.283

The healthcare system in Cote d’Ivoire has suffered from years of conflict and political instability,
which destroyed 42% of health facility. While it was on the mend, then, the country was also
significantly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. However, improving health outcomes is one of
the focuses of the government since the end of the conflict in 2011, with a public expenditure
increase from 1.8 billion USD in 2016 to 2.3 billion USD in 2021.288 Constraints and challenges
remain for women and girls:
• Maternal mortality rates or MMRs: MMR in Cote d’Ivoire is 617 deaths per 100,000 live
births, which is among the highest in the world: only 74% of births are attended by skilled
medical personnel289, and this ratio is remarkably higher in rural areas compared with
urban areas. In 2014, in fact, UNFPA reported 278,801 unattended births in rural areas,
compared with 32,538 in urban areas.290
• Abortion and SRHR: Abortion is illegal in Cote d’Ivoire, except to save a woman’s life.
Unsafe abortions are common and seem to contribute to the very high MMR in the country.
A recent study291 found that the average one-year likely-abortion incidence in Cote
d’Ivoire was 27.9 per 1,000 women of reproductive age for respondents and 40.7 per 1,000
based on confidante data. The majority of abortions in the last five years could be
classified as most unsafe: 71.5% for respondents and 79.9% for confidantes. Among both
groups, women living in rural areas, women with lower levels of education and poorest
women all reported higher rates of unsafe abortions. The modern contraceptive
prevalence for all women aged 15-49 is 22.50%, and the adolescent fertility rate is very
high: between 2012 and 2013 UNFPA reports 5,076 students becoming pregnant while in
primary or secondary school, a significant increase from the previous monitoring
(2007/2008), when 1,292 became pregnant.292
• OECD SIGI report293 on Cote d’Ivoire reports that 75% of the legal framework on violence
against women is in place. 48% of female population justifies domestic violence, which

8.5 Democratic Republic of Congo
The Democratic Republic of Congo (henceforth DRC) is the largest country in Sub-Saharan Africa,
and it is estimated it has the third largest population of poor people globally. The country is rich
in resources, including minerals, metals and agriculture commodity. Agriculture, forestry and
fisheries accounts for approximately 20% of GDP and employ 64% of the population. Key value
chains include cocoa, coffee, rice, maize, cassava, bran, tobacco and palm oil. For the &Green
Fund, plantation forestry and grains staples are priority value chains in DRC, where the fund
aims at establishing a JECA agreement.
8.5.1 Supply chain sectors
Plantation Forestry
60% of the Congo Basin, Africa’s most important rainforest, is located in DRC. While it is mostly
untouched, exploitation of forestry resources is often the only source of livelihood for many of
the 45 million poor people (2019) who live in the country. DRC is one of the least electrified
countries in the world, and it is estimated308 that 84% of all harvested wood in the country is used
for domestic energy consumption. The need for plantation forestry, which can provide wood for
biomass projects, as well as create livelihoods and jobs opportunities for local populations, is
therefore very clear. Since 2018, the Forets project, implemented by CIFOR309 and funded by
European Union in the Yangambi Biosphere Reserve, achieved the plantation of 1 million tree in
2021, with a goal of restoring 2000 hectares of land by 2022. Since the beginning of the project,
more than 1,800 direct jobs have been created.310
Forestry, as in many other countries, is gendered in DRC. Access to and ownership of land is
severely restricted to women: formal land titles giving access to individual ownership are rare,
and procedures are very costly and complex. Most families only have “receipts”, which are issued
to the head of household, who are stipulated as having to be a male. In the case of customary
systems, land is usually attributed through belonging to a clan or lineage, which is established by
men, as it is them who inherit and succeed to their elders in positions of power. In addition to
that, the inter-generational transfer of land takes place through patrilineal inheritance: women
who go and live with the husband’s family cultivate their land, but they do not inherit or acquire
the rights of his clan for themselves. Single women remain under guardianship of their parents or
family members, and widows do not have a right to inherit. Land-use rights for agriculture are
entitled through land-clearing, which clearly advantages men over women, as well as over other
forests groups who do not cultivate the land.311
Division of labour and allocation of time is also influenced by gender norms, with women confined
to subsistence crops, while men monopolise cash crops, and the income they produce. Women are
also tasked with chores that are considered physically lighter, but more constant and time-

consuming (weeding, sowing, seed selection and preparation). Women are recognised as being
more knowledgeable than men in non-timber forest products, as is the case in many other
countries, but have less time than men to organize gathering expeditions. Household work, in fact,
is exclusively a burden of women, which are however excluded from decision making and control
over resources, despite the fact that they play a large and essential role in agricultural labour. To
compound time poverty, men have a right to retire, whereas women continue to work in their old
age.312
Grains and staples
As one of the largest countries in the world by area, including the second largest in Africa, it
produces an enormous volume of agricultural commodities, with much of it consumed
domestically. For example, more than 41 million tonnes of cassava across 5 million hectares of
land were produced in 2020 and 2.3 million tonnes of rice across 1.3 million hectares, yet neither
commodity is an export revenue generator.
In spite of the significant production, the sector fails to ensure food security and generate
sufficient revenues. With 80 million hectares of arable land, 4 million hectares of irrigated land,
and many rivers with important fishery resources, the DRC has the potential to become a global
agricultural power. For the moment, though, the sector lacks commercial agriculture at scale
with most being either smallholders or subsistence farming.
A large proportion of Congolese women are involved in agricultural activity (more than 70% at the
national level), but they are significantly discriminated within the sector. As discussed above,
women experience extreme challenges in accessing and owning land (less than 10% of women are
landowners in DRC), as well as accessing financial services: only 2% of women manage to access
credit, which leaves 42% of women taking loans from friends and family, to be refunded with
exorbitant interest rates. As seen above, women are also discriminated in terms of allocation of
labour, and are systematically excluded from cash crops – they might play a role in the production
chain, but have no access to the income generated.313
Several projects and programmes have focused in the last few years on improving the living
conditions and livelihoods opportunities of women farmers in DRC, such as the UNWOMEN flaghips
programme “Women’s Empowerment through Climate-Smart Agriculture”. The programme was
launched in 2016 focusing on four key areas: access to land, access to climate-smart information,
increase women farmers’ access to finance, increase women farmers’ access to higher value
markets.314 The &Green Fund will leverage on the progress achieved so far, and will continue to
work on the issues and challenges that women farmers face on a daily basis in DRC, with a focus
on those four areas.

The healthcare system in DRC has been under long-term pressure due to conflict, limited
resources, insufficient skilled medical personnel and medical facilities and equipment. While
improvements have been noted in the last few years, thanks to a higher level of stability, many
constraints remain, in particular for women and girls:
• Maternal mortality rates or MMRs: MMR in DRC is 473 per 100,000 live births, which is lower
than the Sub-Saharan Africa average of 534 but still much higher than the WHO target to
reduce MMR to less than 70 deaths for every 100,000 live births. Under-5 mortality rate is
also higher than the SSA average, at 85 deaths for 1,000 live births against 76. A study
reports how conflict-affected areas of the country have seen a continuous decline in
maternal healthcare coverage, particularly among the poorest women.344
• Abortion and SRHR: Abortion is illegal in DRC under almost all circumstances. This means
safe termination is largely inaccessible throughout the country. A study estimated that in
2016 146,700 abortions took place in Kinshasa. In the same year, 33,870 women received
treatment for post-abortion complications. 93% of post-abortion services were provided in
private facilities. Poor women were found to be twice as likely to develop moderate and
serious complications than better-off women. 345 USAID estimates that in 2019
approximately 40.6% of women had an unmet need for family planning, meaning they
wanted to avoid pregnancy but were not using modern contraception methods.346
• Adolescent fertility rate is also very high in DRC: according to the National Institute of
Statistics, the country has more than 21 million adolescents between 10 and 19 years old,
and the median age at first sexual intercourse is 16. Almost 27% of women aged 20 to 24
have given birth by age 18, and almost 5% by age 15, according to the Demographic and
Health Survey 2013-2014.

Women in DRC experience a significant gender gap in accessing economic opportunities, economic
independence and empowerment. Nationally, women are 6.2% to 8.2% less likely to work than
their male counterparts, partly because of the higher number of dependants and, therefore, of
unpaid care work performed.355 Some key elements of disparity include:
• Women employed in agriculture are more than half of the workforce, and yet men own three
quarters of the plots. Women also tend to own smaller plots, which contributes to lower
agricultural productivity, estimated to 11% lower than men, for an overall level of production
18% lower compared with male-owned land. Drivers of this gap could include higher
dependency ratio, lower ownership of land and cell phones, lower number of workers and
lower likelihood to cultivate rice.356
• In the private sector, women’s business profits are 67% lower than men’s, and women’s
business have 70% fewer paid workers. Lower number of workers and low level of capital
emerged as key reasons to explain the gap.357
• Less than 10% of women are waged and salaried, compared with 25% of men. In terms of
wage gap, the national average gap in earning is 77%, and even more pronounced in the
private sector, where it reaches 80%. This can be partly explained by lower level of
educational attainment, skills and concentration in lower paying sectors.358

8.6 Ecuador
Ecuador is a middle-income country, which has made significant progress to reduce poverty and
inequality reduction: the GDP grew on average by 4.3% between 2006 and 2014, poverty went
from 37.6% to 22.5%, and the GINI coefficient decreased from 0.54 to 0.47. However, the COVID-
19 pandemic and the fluctuation of oil price, of which Ecuador is an exporter (the fifth largest in
Latin America in 2020359), have caused poverty to increase again in 2020, reaching 33%.360
IFAD estimates361 that rural population still accounts to approximately 36.5% of the total, and that
61% of rural women works in agriculture and livestock. Agriculture, forestry and fishing
represented 9.8% of GDP in 2020362: key value chains include bananas and white shrimps, of which
Ecuador is the largest exporter in the world, as well as maize, manioc, potato, soybean, coffee,
palm oil, cocoa and more. For the &Green Fund, forestry is a priority value chain in the
country, where the Fund has an active JECA.
8.6.1 Supply chain sectors
Plantation forestry
Ecuador is one of the 17 megadiverse countries of the world, and its rainforest cover almost 13
million hectares – by comparison, an area larger than Greece.363 Forests can be divided into 4 main
groups: Amazon rainforest (approximately 80% of the total), mountainous forests, tropical coastal
rainforest and mangrove forest.364
Out of the total forest coverage, 11.5 million hectares constitute natural forest and 78,000
hectares plantations, representing 42% of the total national surface area.365 Despite its rich
biodiversity, deforestation rate in Ecuador was 1.5% between 1990 and 2000, and increased to
1.9% between 2005 and 2010, for a variety of drivers, including: illegal logging, extractive
industries, cattle ranching and agricultural expansion. Approximately 2 million m³ of industrial
wood consumption (out of a total 3.7 million) are plantation grown.366 The timber industry
amounted, in 2019, to 304 million USD of exportations.367
The main activity of women in rural areas, and in particular in the Amazon, is agriculture and
livestock; they maintain a tight link with their territory and, as observed in other countries, they
lead conservation efforts. Nevertheless, there is an evident gender imbalance: in 2019, the UN
estimated that rural women poverty rate was 35.5%, against the 15.5% national average, and while
they are present in productive processes, they are excluded from decision-making and access to

Gender gaps in terms of enrolment and attainment are very small in Ecuador, but there are still
challenges for women and girls, especially indigenous women and women living in rural areas, to
access and complete their education:
• The World Bank reports393 that reverse gender gaps exist favouring girls in primary and
secondary education, while slightly more men enrol in tertiary education than women. The
gap is reversed, however, at attainment level, where 14.2% of women compared with 12%
of men had post-secondary education.
• Up to 51% of indigenous girls are not enrolled in secondary education, and there is a large
disparity that favours men in secondary enrolment rates.394
• Women still tend to specialize in traditional female fields (education, social work, health,
economy and finance), whereas three quarters of science and engineering students are
men. Moreover, reasons to not be in school are very different between boys and girls: while
the former report work and economic problems as main constraints, the latter also report
dedication to household chores as equally important. Girls also indicate family prohibition
as a reason, which boys do not report395.

Between 2007 and 2017 Ecuador initiated am ambitious healthcare reform, introducing
comprehensive insurance policies, gradually making all Ministry of Health services free of
charge.400 Health coverage was expanded, especially in rural areas, and health inequality
reduction could be observed.401 However, critics notice that the cost recovery mechanisms
established between the public and private sector mainly benefited large private sector hospitals,
and that the opportunity to establish a single health system was gradually fading.402 There is a
clear gendered dimension to access to health, despite significant gains in the last two decades:
• Maternal mortality rates or MMRs: Ecuador has been very successful in lowering maternal
mortality from 96 deaths per 100,000 births to 57 in 2018. Access to antenatal care and
presence of a skilled healthcare professional have increased, however the data shows
inequalities between indigenous and non-indigenous women. In 2018, MMR for indigenous
women was 117 deaths per 100,000 births, due to a variety of reasons, including that
indigenous woman feel discriminated against, and feel a lack of respect for their
traditional birthing practices.403 In 2014, only 14% of indigenous women received the
appropriate minimum five ante-natal check-ups.404
• Abortion: Abortion is illegal in Ecuador, except when the life of the mother is in danger.
Very recently, following a constitutional court ruling, Ecuadorian legislators voted to de-
criminalise abortions in case of rape. Following the vote, and pending approval from the
President, the Law would allow women above 18 years old to terminate pregnancies in
case of rape up to 12 weeks, whereas girls under 18, as well as indigenous and rural
women, would have up to 16 weeks to terminate their pregnancy. 405
• Reproductive health: approximately 79.4% of women’s demand for modern family planning
methods is satisfied, according to WHO. The report indicates some critical gaps for the
fulfilment of SRHR, including stock-out of male condoms in the last 12 months and 41.7%
availability of essential medicines and commodities in Public Health facilities – this reflects
the lack of pharmacists among the healthcare professionals, who are 0.42 per 10,000
population.406

8.7 Gabon
Gabon is an upper-middle-income country in Africa. The fifth largest oil producer in the continent,
it has had strong economic growth over the past decade, driven by its production of oil and
manganese.427 Gabon is a highly-forested nation, with 85 – 88% forest cover, and houses
approximately 18% of the Congo-Ogooué Basin’s forest.428 These forests remain relatively intact
and are globally important as a reservoir for biodiversity and a sink for atmospheric CO .
2
Employment in agriculture remains high in Gabon – about 30% of the working population, and
attracts 46% of the total female labour force participation, despite entrenched industries and
satellite services around extractives in the country. Gabon has adopted a series of reforms to its
civil and penal codes designed to give women more rights in the home and at work. Among other
things, the reforms make it possible for any woman to open a bank account and go to work without
the permission of her husband. As a result, Gabon’s score on the Women, Business and the Law
2022 index rose to 82.5, a substantial increase from 57.5 two years prior. The &Green Fund has
an active JECA in Gabon, and will work towards addressing gender barriers identified in the
local contexts through its investments.
8.7.1 Supply chain sectors
Plantation forestry
The forestry sector is a significant contributor to Gabon’s economy.429 In 2016, GDP for forest
exploitation was CFAF 91.1 billion (+21.5%), or 1.1% (0.9%) of national GDP at current prices.430
GDP linked to wood-related industries was CFAF 149 billion (+6.6%), or 1.8% (1.6%) of the national
GDP.431 The entire sector represents CFAF 240.1 billion, or 2.9 percent of national GDP.432
Timber exports are Gabon’s second main export after oil and manganese, accounting for roughly
nine percent of the country’s total value of exports. Gabon exports USD 248 million in sawn wood
annually, making it the third largest export revenue generator behind petroleum and manganese
ore.433 The main destinations for sawn wood are China (USD 218 million), Belgium (USD 16.8
million), Italy (USD 7.6 million) and France (USD 7.3 million).434 Approximately 10.7 million
hectares of Gabon’s 21 million hectares of rainforest are allocated as concessions for commercial
timber production.

Currently, Gabon-specific gender studies on plantation and agroforestry is limited, although the
Congo Basin Forest Partnership435 has recently launched gender consultations on women’s rights
in the forestry sectors of Gabon and Congo. Research is currently underway (conducted around
three provinces of Gabon – Estuaire, Ngounié, and Nyanga) into the bush mango value chain –
which reveal that women-headed household rely on this as an important source of revenue.436
Kiptot and Franzel (2012) explore these issues broadly in Africa from a gender perspective,
examining women’s participation relative to men and the challenges and successes they
experience.437
Particular agroforestry practices examined include fodder production and utilization, soil fertility
management, woodlots and indigenous fruit and vegetable production and processing. The review
shows that agroforestry has the potential to offer substantial benefits to women; however, their
participation is low in enterprises that are considered men’s domain, such as timber and high in
enterprises that have little or no commercial value, such as collection of indigenous fruits and
vegetables.438
Furthermore, the degree of women’s involvement relative to men in technologies such as soil
fertility management, fodder production and woodlots is fairly high in terms of proportion of
female-headed households participating but is low as measured by the area they allocate to these
activities and the number of trees they plant. Data on whether women are able to manage
agroforestry practices as well as men are mixed, although it is clear that women do most of the
work but are not remunerated adequately.439 In cases where they do not perform well, the reasons
are mostly due to scarcity of resources. In marketing, women are also confined to the lower end
of the value chain (retailing), which limits their control over and returns from the productive
process.

Gabon spends approximately 3.44% of its GDP on health care (2014) which is comparatively less
than neighboring countries.454 Despite this level of spending, Gabon has managed to expand its
health coverage through the national healthcare system (the Caisse Nationale d’Assurance Maladie
et de Garantie Sociale) by levying taxes on mobile phone companies and money transfers coming
from abroad.455 Despite this social protection system, Gabonese women continue facing significant
challenges to their health that include:
• A high rate of maternal mortality (252 in 2017) which is far higher than the rate of 20
maternal deaths per 100,000 live births that the WHO deems acceptable. Here again, there
are large rural-urban difference with respect to coverage with 94% of urban women
delivering in a health structure compared to 70% of rural women.456 Prior data from 1998
on MMR suggests that most hospitalisations occurred due to malaria which is endemic in
Gabon.457

8.8 Indonesia
Indonesia is a developing economy with abundant natural resources, and has employed its
endowments, including forests – as a means towards development and improved economic
benefits. This is reflected in Global Forest Watch’s forest change data: in 2001, Indonesia had
93.8Mha of primary forest, extending over 50% of its land area. In 2021, it lost 203Kha of primary
forest, equivalent to 157Mt of CO Activities that contribute to deforestation include unplanned
2.
felling of natural forest timber at concessions; the conversion of forested areas due to agricultural
expansion (estate crops), mining, plantations and transmigration, unsustainable forest
management, illegal logging, encroachment and illegal land occupation in forested areas.
Deforestation and forest degradation in Indonesia, therefore, are inseparable from Indonesia’s
political economy.484
The Indonesian government’s commitment to include gender mainstreaming in national
development was sealed in 2000 through a mandate designed to trickle down into all policies and
programs in all ministries. Even before it merged with the Ministry of Environment, the Ministry
of Forestry embraced gender mainstreaming, also weaving it throughout policies and programs, a
practice that has since continued. Women are encouraged to participate in projects through the
Pangarusutamaan Gender (PUG) program, designed to mainstream gender into forest and
environmental policies, including those targeting forest tenure.
The country’s political economy, however, continues to experience gender barriers: Indonesia has
made significant progress on several dimensions of gender equality, including achieving gender
parity in net enrollment rates, and expanding basic health services. However, these improvements
have not yet translated into increased economic participation of women. Indonesia’s female
labour force participation rates have remained low and stubbornly stagnant over the last two
decades, at around 52% (against labour force participation rates of men around 85%).485 Indonesia
is also the world’s largest archipelago – approximately 6,000 islands are populated among the total
17,000: making it a geographically vast and a diverse country, with intersections of gender,
ethnicity, and religion. These diverse social markers combine with systematic welfare as well as
disparities across groups, which has a cascading effect on agrocommodities and value chains.
For the &Green Fund, particularly in the context of priority value chains: palm oil, rubber and
plantation forestry, these issues are relevant. The Fund has a country-level JECA active in
Indonesia since November 8, 2021.486
8.8.1 Supply chain sectors
Palm oil
Indonesia is the world’s number one producer of palm oil – and has witnessed zero-deforestation
commitments in this particular supply chain, although implementation problems remain rife. For
example, in 2014, two groups or coalitions of major palm oil producers with overlapping
memberships emerged – the Indonesian Palm Oil Pledge (IPOP) and the Sustainable Palm Oil

=== PAGE 239 ===
Page 235
Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
Manifesto (SPOM).487 Aside from deforestation, they have attempted to address social issues
explicitly as well as land rights, conflicts and smallholder issues – which indirectly impact forest
loss in Indonesia. Research undertaken by World Rainforest Movement has revealed that gendered
exploitation and discrimination in the palm oil industry is an ongoing phenomenon, although the
extent is difficult to estimate. These dynamics can range from lower/no pay for the same work,
sexual harassment and gender-based violence at the workplace, and spillover effects of
environmental impacts of palm oil plantations.
In Indonesia, women and children are often forced to work for free to help men meet the production
targets that the company sets as condition for them to receive the full wage for the day, WRM finds.488
Women, often, tend to be restricted to low-paying, arduous and demeaning tasks, including the
spraying of pesticides. These are tasks that are extremely dangerous for women and their reproductive
health.489 Gender-based violence in the palm oil supply chain has remained insidious: 490 women have
reported rape and torture in or around the plantation fields, with the perpetrators usually going
unpunished. In addition, violent arrests or searches have been conducted by private sector entities
arguing that palm nuts or palm oil have been stolen from the company plantations. This comes with
women having their traditional oil production taken away or destroyed, in many cases.
Research conducted by Stockholm Environment Institute in the Central Kalimantan Province has
revealed that local communities have severe grievances about the impacts of oil palm plantations
on water resources.491 Plantations affect both water quality and quantity – for example by
polluting drinking water and drying community wells. Women are often responsible for household
water provision, and strain on water resources often force them (and girls) to travel long distances
to access water. This has the dual impact of increasing their drudgery, as well as higher exposure
to the risk of sexual assault or violently searched.
Rubber
Indonesia is the world’s second-largest producer of rubber, and has the highest acreage under
rubber cultivation globally. The land-use change that has fueled this expansion has had significant
impacts on Indonesian forests (particularly in Jambi and other parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan of the
Borneo region) as well as socioeconomic features.
When rubber was recognized as an increasingly lucrative commodity, the division of labour in
agricultural land between women and men were sedimented. Women were generally responsible
for subsistence agriculture in rice fields and homesteads, while men were responsible for rubber
production and marketing.492 Rubber trees are usually tapped every day, so labour input is
constantly required. Male and female household members are both involved in rubber cultivation

Through its programming, the &Green Fund will ensure marginalized producers within the rubber

the due diligence stage. Where possible, the Fund will work with IDH to increase technical support
to companies to increase social inclusion as well as capacity.
Plantation forestry
Plantation forests require intensive management, but they grow faster than natural forests: in
2011 FAO reported that although they accounted only for 5% of the total wood forest area, it
produced 35% of all the world’s wood product.495 Indonesia has made several attempts to promote
sustainable management and commercialisation of forests, and currently it is one of several
countries in the world leading the way in the design and implementation of REDD+ (Reducing
Emission from Deforestation and Forest Degradation). Indonesia is in the second phase of
implementing policy reforms and REDD+ pilots and transitioning towards the third phase of
performance-based payments.496 Indonesia has also established the community plantation forests
(CPF) programme in 2007 by the Ministry of Forestry with the aim of increasing community
involvement in forest utilisation.497
8.8.2 Latest Global Gender Gap Index score
Indonesia has closed 68.8% of its overall gender gap, corresponding to a rank of 101st globally,
although the gap this year is 1.3 percentage points larger than in the previous edition. This decline
has resulted mainly from wider Economic Participation and Opportunity gaps where the country
has lost 4 percentage points since last year, regressing to a gap currently closed of 64.7%. This
can be explained almost exclusively by a sharp drop in the share of women in senior roles, which
halved from 54.9% to 29.8% in just one year. Beyond the performance of this indicator, women
participate in the labour market significantly less than men (55.9% of women and 84% of men) and
wage and income gaps remain large (69.7% and 51.7%, respectively). In addition, 81.8% of the
women’s employment is in the informal sector (compared to 79.4% of men).
Indonesia’s GGGI score in 2021 was 0.688, which means it ranks 10th at the regional level and 101
globally. Sub-scores are as follows:

• Abortion: abortion is allowed in Indonesia only in case of medical emergency, or severe
anomaly of the foetus (for which, however, consent from both husband and wife is
required). In 2009 the law was expanded to allow abortion after rape, but only within 6
weeks of gestation. The Guttmacher Institute reports that most abortion take place outside
of these strict conditions, and the majority are unsafe. The Institute also reports that in
the Java Province, in 2018, 73% of women seeking an abortion self-managed.526
• SRHR: It should be noted that from 1970 to 2002 Indonesia experienced significant gains in
access to modern contraception. However, contraception prevalence has been stagnant
since then, and remains low in specific regions (such as Papua) and social groups, including
adolescents and unmarried couples, to whom the law forbids the purchase of
contraceptives. In addition, religious and traditional stigma associated with premarital sex
contributes to hamper contraceptive use and access, with only 45% of married or sexually
active adolescents reported as using contraception. Child marriage is also widespread, with
one in nine women been married before age 18: the eighth highest number of child
marriages in the world. 527
• Gender-Based Violence: violence against women is prevalent in Indonesia, at home, in
school, on public transport and in the workplace. According to the 2016 Indonesian National
Women’s Life Experience Survey, one in three Indonesian women (15-64) have experienced
violence in their lifetime, inflicted mostly by their spouses and those who are closest to
them.528 The survey also found that 9 percent of respondents had experienced violence in
the last 12 months. Women are also 13 times more likely than men to be abused in public
transport than men529, and there is emerging evidence of women not reporting harassment
on the workplace, due to fear of potential repercussions.530

8.9 Lao PDR
The Lao People’s Democratic Republic (henceforth, Lao) has obtained significant development
progress between 2000 and 2010, halving poverty, reducing malnutrition, and improving health
and educational outcomes. However, since 2013 economic growth has slowed, and the effects of
the COVID-19 pandemic might reverse some of the gains achieved so far.
Agriculture is a key part of Laos’ economy, accounting for 16.2% of GDP in 2020. Approximately
two-thirds of the population live in rural areas, most of which are employed in agriculture. The
main sources of agricultural export revenue are bananas, cassava and coffee beans. For the
&Green Fund, coffee and plantation forestry are a priority value chain in Lao, where the fund
aims at establishing a JECA agreement.
8.9.1 Supply chain sectors
Coffee
Coffee has become one Laos’ three main agricultural exports and has contributed to reducing
poverty in parts of the country544. The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry has set a goal of
increasing coffee production to 1 million tons by 2025.
There is a promising market opportunity for the Lao coffee sector, as the local and regional
demand for coffee are increasing. Viet Nam imports on average 50% of Lao’s total Arabica coffee
beans every year, and China and India have also come on board as new potential market
opportunities. Domestic demand for coffee has been increasing as well. The launch of many new
coffee shops /cafés as well as small-scale roasters in recent years is an indicator of the increasing
popularity of Lao coffee among locals. Some established coffee brands such as Sinouk Coffee, Lao
Mountain Coffee, Saffron Coffee, Le Trio Coffee, Meuang Xieng Coffee, Yumi Coffee, and Dao
Coffee are marketed locally, hoping that the booming tourism can boost their sales545.
The quality of Lao’s coffee has been improving and is slowly gaining market recognition. This has
been aided in part by technical support from development partners such as the Agence Française
de Développement (AFD) and GIZ. The private sector is also playing an important role in
introducing and developing clean agriculture to be able to export Lao coffee through large retail
networks across the globe546. There are more than 20,000 smallholder families making a living
from selling coffee beans, and more than 300,000 people (or about 6 per cent of the total working
age population) engaged in jobs linked to the coffee industry.
Coffee value chain actors in Laos include:
• Agricultural input providers: supply the main agricultural inputs (machinery, equipment,
fertilizers and seedlings). They also perform other roles, including collecting, trading and
exporting coffee and other crops.
544 https://www.afd.fr/en/actualites/laos-increasingly-sustainable-coffee-production
545 UNCTAD (2020)
546
E Co. 107

=== PAGE 247 ===
Page 243
Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
• Coffee producers can be divided into two groups: i) independent or individual smallholder
farmers, groups and cooperatives; and ii) large-scale commercial coffee producers (many
of which were established by foreign investors.
• Coffee traders: Small-scale coffee traders play an important role in collecting and selling
coffee to big companies like Dao Hueang Group, Thin Nghia, Cat Que, and Pakse. It has
been reported that Viet Namese companies are being increasingly active in coffee trading
in the province.
Coffee production is gendered in Lao, as observed in similar countries: a study547 focusing on
Arabica coffee production and women’s decision-making highlights that, while women are
included in the production chain, the division of labour is shaped by gender norms. Men tend to
focus on pruning and on other tasks involving machines, while women on picking and sorting, which
is physically lighter but also more time-consuming.
The study examines how the introduction of the New Economic Mechanism (NEM – which started
the economic liberalisation process) in 1986 drove a shift in agricultural production, which in turn
had the effect of engaging women more in farming work. While economic growth has brought gains
in terms of decision-making and empowerment, the study finds that men hold more decision-
making power on land acquisition, technology use, fertiliser application, labour hiring, harvesting,
and borrowing of money from a bank or money lender. Importantly, though, the analysis shows
that women and men have equal decision-making power in the household on selling farm products
and education of children.
The &Green Fund will focus on expanding the role of women in coffee production, strengthening
their decision-making and increasing access to training and resources to avoid a perpetration of
gendered division of labour. It will be important also to acknowledge and address the dual burden
of women in the fields and in the household, decreasing the time poverty of women farmers in
order to give more relevance to their role in the community and in the production chain.
Plantation forestry
Lao has a policy target of reaching 70% of forest cover by 2020. In 2018, the cover stood at 58%548,
and plantation forests, which have considerably expanded in the last few years, represented 1.7%
of the overall forest coverage.549 Plantation forests are mostly made of teak, rubber, eucalypt and
acacia trees. The ownership rates vary significantly based on the type of trees: teak plantations
are 99% owned by smallholder farmers, whereas 48.7% of rubber plantations are owned through
company concessions, 24.7% through contract farming and the remaining 28.5% by smallholder
farmers. Finally, 88.3% of eucalypt and acacia plantations are owned through company
concessions, 10.4% through contract farming and only 1.3% by smallholder farmers.550

making power in coffee-farming households in Lao PDR. Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 26(1) p. 49-71. ISSN: 1823-
4127

Gender norms shaping the Laotian society are diverse, and vary depending on the main ethnic
groups (Lao-Tai, Mon-Khmer, Hmon Lu-Mien, Chine-Tibetan). Non Lao-Tai women seem to
experience additional challenges compared with Lao-Tai women, which are the predominant group
in the country (67%) and are reported as having more equal gender norms compared with the other
three main groups.551 When it comes to access to land, cultural norms are key as customary law
will be enforced differently whether a village or a community is matrilineal (ensuring protection
of women to inherit and own land) or patrilineal (which only transfers land to men, meaning
women can only access it through marriage, and only sons can inherit it). Lao-Tai and to some
extent Mon-Khmer communities appear to be mostly matrilineal, and to sustain customary law,
empowering women to negotiate and to uphold their rights.552
Among other key barriers preventing women from participating equally and fully to forestry
community life, the following can be listed: i) women are reported as having limited
representation in community forestry initiatives, meaning forestry decision-making is made
without consideration of women’s needs; ii) although in 2021 Lao, with support from SIDA,
unveiled a strategy to strengthen gender mainstreaming in forestry553, female forest officials are
still very uncommon, including due to security risks for crossing long distances; iii) Social and
linguistic barriers, especially for women of non Lao-Tai ethnic groups, can hamper participation.
Also, unpaid care work is a significant obstacle for women to participate actively in activities out
of the household; iv) Access to capital and resources is limited for women, and men dominate the
value chain, highlighting a lack of power and knowledge of women in terms of pricing, negotiation
and types of timber.554
On the other hand, women’s involvement in forestry has been linked with: i) a decrease in illegal
activity; ii) increased representation in decision-making, as well as a tendency to sanction and
exclude less, reducing conflict and increasing effective forest management; iii) mobilization of
people for collective action, and better access to information from external agents; iv) increased
commitment and interest to protect the forest.555
The &Green Fund will strive to acknowledge these barriers, and to work on sustainable forestry
increasing agency, decision-making power and knowledge of women, leveraging on their specific
skills and awareness of non-timber forest products and sustainable use of forestry environments.

Lao has made some remarkable progress in educational attainment and performance in the last
two decades, achieving universal access to primary education. However, in 2015 the public
spending on education was 2.6% of GDP, considerably lower the 4.7% global median, and below
regional neighbours like Viet Nam and Malaysia.577 Specific constraints and disparities remain:
• While universal access to primary education has been achieved, completion rate for basic
education remains low. A 2017 student learning assessment showed that 1 in 3 students in
grade 3 met the literacy standards for promotion to grade 4, and only 1 in 5 met the
standards in math. Similarly, an assessment in 2019 found that students at the lower level
of secondary school (grade 9) do not master literacy and math skills. Few students are
reaching upper secondary. For every 100 students that start Grade 1, only 83 reach Grade
5, 51 reach Grade 9/Mathayom 4, and 33 reach Grade 12/Mathayom 7.578 However, Lao has
nearly achieved gender parity at primary level.579
• Only 60% of children of lower secondary age attend school, and at least 1 in 6 children
(17%) are out of school. The gap is wider in remote and marginalised communities,
including ethnic minorities, households where mothers have low or no educational levels,
and the poorest quintile. In all these communities less than half the children between 11
and 14 attend school, and one quarter are out of school.580
• At secondary level gender parity has not been achieved, and fewer girls than boys are
enrolled. In vulnerable groups, with the exception of Chinese-Tibetan, boys attend school
proportionally more than girls.581 While girls represent now 46% of TVET students, the
selection of subjects is still skewed towards occupations traditionally considered more
“feminine”, such as tailoring, basic business administration and hospitality.582

Lao has made some remarkable progress in health in the last fifteen years. Life expectancy
continuously increased until reaching 66 in 2015, maternal mortality was decreased by 75%,
therefore meeting the MDG target, immunization rate has increased, and the Health Sector Reform
(HSR) saw the introduction of the national health insurance, the reform of the health information
system and the introduction of an essential service package. However, women and girls still face
challenges and constraints:
• Maternal mortality rates or MMRs: although MMR decreased to 185 deaths per 100,000 live
births in 2017, compared with 905 in 1990, it is still above the regional average and far
from the WHO and SDG goal of less than 70 per 100,000 births. Only two thirds of births
are delivered in a health facility and attended by a skill medical professional.588 The World

Chine-Tibetan women). Likewise, while at the national level 44% of mothers and newborns
receive post-natal care, the proportion is lower in the aforementioned groups: 24%, 27%
and 23%, respectively.589

8.10 Liberia
Liberia is rich in natural resources, which include: iron ore, diamonds, gold, fertile soil, fishery,
and forestry. About 50% of Liberians live within 2.5 kilometres of a forest – and each day, these
households spend over three hours collecting forest products for subsistence and for sale, earning
about 35% of their income.604 In case of crisis such as droughts, fires, floods or pandemics, forests
provide a safety net, offering resources to recover from the shocks. Informal and largely
unmeasured, forest activities provide an important source of jobs, income and food security.
Despite the crucial role forests play in sustaining livelihoods, 12.2% of Liberia’s forest cover was
lost from 1990 to 2010.
Women – and men – in Liberia are employed primarily within the agriculture and service sector.605
In some areas such as food crops, female participation exceeds male participation. However,
women in agriculture are largely considered to be unempowered because of key constraints like:
limited autonomy in production. Insecure land ownership and land tenure continue to limit
women’s access to credit, inputs, and, ultimately, productivity and financial empowerment. The
Ebola epidemic (followed by COVID-19 pandemic), the drop in global commodity prices crisis, and
increases in the cost of living that occurred from 2014 to 2015 have had a lingering impact on the
Liberian economy – and particularly on women’s economic empowerment.606 The &Green Fund
has an active JECA in Liberia and will be ensuring that gender issues identified in this
assessment are addressed within the ambit of the investments proposed in the country.
8.10.1 Supply chain sectors
Cocoa
Cocoa is the second largest agricultural revenue generator accounting for more than USD 33 million
in 2020. Liberia has a favourable climate and fertile soil for cocoa production. There has been
substantial investment in the rehabilitation of cooperative and smallholder cocoa farms. The
country’s international partners, such as IFAD, continue to invest in cocoa smallholder producers
to improve livelihoods and raise incomes by modernizing cocoa farming, increasing production,
and developing market access.
Research by Soliridad West Africa607 has revealed the need mainstream gender equality issues in
the cocoa sub-sector across the entire value chain. However, the challenge is to ensure that the
major players in the cocoa sector, that is investors and private companies, are willing to
implement measures towards gender inclusiveness to overcome the status quo. According to a
gender assessment conducted by them, huge gender inequality (especially against women) exists
in the sector. The study revealed that an estimated 75% of the tasks in cocoa cultivation are

Specific efforts to target women cocoa farmers are needed, in order to support these farmers’
essential role in boosting cocoa quality to the levels required on the premium market.608 Cocoa
businesses (including cooperatives, traders, exporters and farmers) are recognizing the mounting
evidence that female farmers are important for cocoa bean quality—in particular because of their
essential roles in post-harvesting activities, such as breaking pods and drying and fermenting cocoa
beans. It is also widely recognized that female farmers tend to have higher training needs than
their male counterparts. Yet, numerous interventions implemented to promote cocoa
sustainability continue to be gender blind, and limit opportunities for women working effectively
and benefitting equitably from this value chain in Liberia.
Palm oil
Palm oil is another significant cash crop in Liberia. Traditionally, it is a domestically consumed
product but there has been some export development with smallholders and large investors
expressing interest in expanding cash crop production. Nevertheless, the Central Bank of Liberia’s
2020 report showed a slight decline in palm oil production (from 22,465 metric tons to 22,200
metric tons) due to limited labour mobility because of COVID-19 related restrictions.
The Government of Liberia developed a National Oil Palm Export Strategy (2014-2018) aimed at
enhancing the productive capacity in the palm oil sector, particularly at the smallholder level
through the outgrowers’ scheme.609 The strategy proposes the establishment of an integrated
research programme and to augment the availability of quality skilled and semi-skilled labour to
improve business services and extension services support.610
An important issue that needs to be addressed to mobilise this strategy relates to gender equity
and inclusion – the roles and responsibilities that men, women and youth play in every aspect of
the oil palm value chain.
Both men and women play critical roles in the oil palm value chain. However, women contribute
more to processing and marketing, while men do the harvest at the smallholder level. One of the
strategies for achieving the objectives of the Oil Palm Export Strategy that the government is to
ensure that the outgrower schemes allocate land to women. The strategy should address
appropriate land rights and utilisation mechanisms to reduce land conflicts between
concessionaires and local communities that cut across gender as men, women and youth aspire to
protect their land. There is an urgent need to develop gender-sensitive indicators that specifically
identify, document and close the data gap on women’s activities along the palm oil value chain.

Rubber
Rubber is a dominant revenue generator, accounting for 13.5 percent of total export receipts in
2020. Liberia is the largest producer of natural rubber in Africa, accounting for USD 102 million in
2020 and producing nearly 65,000 tonnes on 87,000 hectares. Various estimates put the number
of people employed by commercial rubber farms at 22,000 and the number of smallholder
households involved in growing rubber trees at 38,000.
Women and youth constitute a significantly proportion of the labour force on the rubber
plantations and private rubber farms across the country.611 They provide labour for clearing,
planting, crop maintenance as well as harvest to some extent. The policy framework for natural
rubber is embedded in the concession agreements with large producers which do not clearly
address gender issues. Generally, gender equality issues in the rubber sector are based the labour
laws of Liberia such as the Decent Work Bill, National Social Protection Policy, and other policies
for gender inclusion. Concessions are expected to adhere to Liberia gender policies. However,
there are no clear indicators to be used as yardsticks for monitoring gender inclusiveness and
empowerment in the rubber sector.
8.10.2 Latest Global Gender Gap Index score
Liberia has closed 69.3% of its overall gender gap, achieving a rank of 94th globally. Only 54.4% of
Liberia’s literacy gender gap has been bridged with a literacy rate of 34.1% for women against
62.7% for men explaining its low ranking with regard to the overarching Educational Attainment
gender gap category (83.9% of the gap has been bridged).
Liberia’s GGGI score in 2021 was 0.693, which means it ranks 15th at the regional level and 94th
globally. Sub-scores are as follows:

to 40.1 percent of their male counterparts. For every 100,000 live births, 661.0 women die from

In the last two decades Liberia has made progress in improving the health and quality of life
prospects for its citizens. Life expectancy at birth has risen from 52 years in 2000 to 64 years in
2020626.
• Between 2000 and 2019, Liberia’s Human Development Index value increased from 0.435
to 0.480, an increase of 10.3 percent. Despite this increase, Liberia still only ranks 175 /
189 countries. In the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap (2021) Liberia ranked
136 / 156 countries for Health and Survival.
• While the adolescent birth rate (for women between 15 – 19) decreased from 150 women
per 1,000 in 2015 to 128 per 1,000 women aged 15-19 as of 2018627 maternal mortality and
women’s access to quality care remains a major issue. This is particularly acute for rural
women, who are far from health facilities. Although more than 50% of births take place in
a healthcare facility, children born in rural settings are twice as likely to be delivered by
a relative or friend, rather than a skilled provider, as compared to in the greater Monrovia
area.
• The issue of sexual and gender-based violence is attracting growing attention both
internationally and within Liberian society. GbV is widespread and often seen as a private,
family matter. According to the 2019-2020 Liberia Demographic and Health Survey, 60% of
women age 15-49 have experienced physical violence and 9% have experienced sexual
violence. Less than half (42%) of women who have experienced physical or sexual violence
have ever sought help.Rape is one of the most frequently reported crimes in Liberia, and
the rate of sexual violence against women in Liberia is among the highest in the world.
Female Genital Cutting, which is also considered gender-based violence (GBV), is widely
accepted and practiced in Liberia. This remains controversial because it is practiced by
Liberia’s Traditional Sande School and highlights the lack of harmonization between
Liberia’s traditional and national laws and the impact that has on gender roles and
women’s rights628.
