Liberia is still in the process of rebuilding its education system after 14 years of civil war, which
resulted in the destruction of much of country’s trained workforce and 60% of school buildings637.
The 2014 school closure due to the Ebola Viral Disease (EVD) outbreak, has further inhibited the
recovery of the country’s fragile education system.
It has one of the world's highest levels of out-school children, with an estimated 15 to 20 per cent
of 6–14 year-olds who are not in class. Just over a third of pre-schoolers have access to early
childhood learning programmes and only 54 per cent of children complete primary education. For
those children who are enrolled in primary and secondary school, many are overage. In fact, the
vast majority of Liberia’s students are older than the appropriate age for their grade and are
therefore at high risk of dropping out. At present, overage enrollment is a consequence of late
entry into grade one and lack of enforcement of the age appropriate enrolment policy638.
In Liberia there are substantial educational disparities due to gender, rural-urban locality, and
income inequality – with poor rural girls and women being at the greatest disadvantage. Poverty,
discriminatory social and gender norms, lack of sexual health and reproductive rights, and high
levels of sexual and gender-based violence negatively affect girls’ access, retention, and
completion of secondary school in Liberia. In the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap
(2021) Liberia ranked 142 / 156 countries for Educational Attainment639.

The majority of Liberian women are employed informally and in low-productivity sectors,
particularly the agriculture (40% of female employment in 2019) and service sectors. Very few
Liberian women hold position within the professional, managerial, technical or skilled labour
sectors, limiting potential for economic growth.
Despite recent improvements, Liberia’s investment climate still ranks fairly low by international
standards and was ranked 175 / 190 countries in the World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business Report
in 2019. Women in particular encounter several obstacles to doing business in Liberia, including:
• Education — As a result of conflict (see SDG 4), a high proportion of women lack the basic
skills to conduct business successfully and often find themselves in low-productivity jobs.
The prolonged years of conflict led to high rates of illiteracy, particularly among women.
The current generation of women entrepreneurs lacks many of the basic skills needed to
successfully operate a business. Also, lack of technical skills due to the breakdown of the

8.11 Zambia
Zambia is a large, land-locked and resource-rich country, with a sparse and mostly urban
population. While poverty data are not recent, and only available until 2015, the World Bank
recorded a significant contraction of the economy by 2.8% in 2020, with recovery expectation of
3.3% growth in 2021 and 3.8% between 2022 and 2025. However, as a result of the COVID-19 crisis,
the World Bank expected poverty to increase slightly in 2020, reaching 60.8%.651 Agriculture
accounts for approximately 19% of the GDP and employs roughly three quarters of the population.
Main value chains include: maize, sorghum, millet, and cassava while exports are driven by sugar,
soybeans, coffee, groundnuts, rice, and cotton as well as horticultural produce. For the &Green
Fund, grains and staples are a priority value chain in Zambia, where the fund aims at
establishing a JECA agreement.
8.11.1 Supply chain sectors
Grains, staples
Maize is the main staple cultivated in Zambia, with approximately 3,387,470 tonnes produced in
2020 and almost 39 million USD export revenue. According to FAO652, supplies for 2021/22
marketing year are satisfactory: to give an example, in this period, Zambia recorded its largest
corn crop: 3.4 million tonnes, in line with the very good performance of the region, which was
also the main cause for lower export demand from neighbouring countries.653 However, FAO also
flags that poorer rains than expected are hampering 2022 crop prospects, and that while food
insecurity has reduced slightly since the same period last year, 1.6 million people are still in need
of assistance.
While agriculture accounts for a smaller percentage of GDP compared to other similar countries,
mostly due to the relevance of mining, it is the main source of livelihood for 60% of households,
with women providing 70% of agricultural labour.654 It is also a driver of deforestation, especially
in the Eastern Province.655
Farming is gendered in Zambia, with female farmers encountering a number of challenges. Women
suffer from insecure land tenure, both in customary and statutory systems.656 Studies show that
land tenure insecurity translates into reduction of climate smart agriculture practices: in Zambian
households where women have less tenure security, they apply 13–18% less fertilizer, fallow 4–5%
less land area, and use intensive tillage techniques on 3–5% fewer acres.657 There is also evidence

• While the secondary net enrolment rate increased from 25.4% in 2016 to 42.9% in 2017,

Zambia’s healthcare system is based on universal access, although there are significant constraints
to funding and availability of care. The system is decentralised, and broken down in three levels:
hospitals, health centres and health posts. Hospitals are further disaggregated into primary
(district), secondary (provincial) and tertiary (central). There is a clear gendered dimension to
access to health, despite significant gains in the last two decades:
• Maternal mortality rates or MMRs: Zambia has decreased MMR by 300% in 16 years, going
from 729 deaths every 100,000 live births in 2002 to 278 in 2018. This has been mainly
possible by increasing attendance at birth of skilled medical staff, which has gone from
42% in 2002 to 80% in 2018.687 This is however still far from the target of reducing deaths
to 70 every 100,000 births, as enshrined in target 3.1 of SDG 3. Early marriage decreased
from 42% in 2002 to 31.4% in 2014, which shows progress, but still a significant incidence.
Adolescent pregnancy is also high, and significantly higher in rural area compared with
urban area (37% vs 20% in 2014) leading to school drop-out and exposure to health risks.
Moreover, 86% of girls who become pregnant while in school are between 10 and 14 years
old.688

9. National policy environment and legal
framework for gender-transformative
investments
Around the world, gender and social inequalities impedes women, girls, and other marginalized
social groups in terms of economic opportunities, endowments, and access to assess – limiting
their development pathways. In the &Green target countries, gender relations are varied – women
are taking the lead in certain value chains (such as the niche sustainable coffee value chain in
Peru), and play limited roles in certain value chains (such as cattle in Mexico). Men – particularly
indigenous men in Latin America – are agricultural workers, and are faced with complex gendered
realities as well.
In terms of national policy and legal frameworks, although most countries have progressive or
gender-neutral laws – there is still a trend to reify discrimination against women and girls in
respect to men and boys and unequal power relations. The formalization in laws and replication
in practices and traditions perpetuates the cycle of discrimination, which becomes cemented into
social institutions that are transmitted from generation to generation.
Decades of research have proven that promoting gender equality in education, employment and
health not only delivers benefits for women but for whole communities and economies. The lever
for improving outcomes is improved legal and policy frameworks at national levels – as well as
their percolation to devolved levels of governance.
This section uses the OECD Development Centre’s Social Institutions and Gender Index (SIGI)
research. The SIGI is an innovative measure of discriminatory social institutions.698 The SIGI’s
indicators address the de jure and de facto situations of discriminatory social institutions across
five sub-indices: discriminatory family code, restricted physical integrity, son bias, restricted
resources and assets and restricted civil liberties. Since existing gender indicators commonly focus
on key economic and social indicators, like employment or education, the SIGI focuses on social
norms, offering an analytical lens to explain persistent gaps in these outcomes between women
and men.
This section also tabulates when the 17 target countries ratified the:
CEDAW: Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; and the
CERD: International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, which
remain milestone international commitments towards improved gender and racial equality
globally. Further information can be found on the UN Treaty Body Database.
698 Methodology note on the SIGI: https://www.oecd.org/dev/development-gender/Backgroundpaper_cover.pdf
Developed by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development

Brazil
Key institution Ministry of Women, Family and Human Rights
Brazil’s Civil Code determines that women and men have the same
rights regarding land and resources. The presidential decree No. 759,
which complements the Land Statute (Lei 4.504-64) and the Agrarian
Law (Lei 8629-93), establishes that women and families headed by
women should be given priority in receiving land titles.
Land rights
Notwithstanding the provisions protecting women’s land ownership
rights, local customs commonly infringe the enjoyment of women’s
land rights over inheritance or after divorce (UN Women Brazil, 2015).
An agricultural census research from the government on land property
in 2006 found that women represented only 13% of farm and
agricultural establishment owners (UN Women Brazil, 2015).
Women have the same rights as men to open a bank account and
obtain credit at a financial institution (Federal Constitution, Article
5). This article takes precedence before every legislation in the
Financial rights
country. Any discrimination in matters related to access to credit,
opening banking accounts or access to formal financial institution are
thus excluded and unconstitutional.
CEDAW The CEDAW was ratified on 01 February 1984.
CERD The CERD was ratified on 27 March 1968.
Cameroon
Key institution Cameroon Ministry of Women's Empowerment and the Family
In principle, the state’s Constitution affords each citizen the right to
own property individually or jointly with other (Art. 17, 1992).
Moreover, the law states that no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of
their property (Ibid). However, these rights are hindered by other
discriminatory laws, both in civil and customary legal regimes that do
not allow married women to own or manage land and assets. Namely,
Land rights
under civil law, marital property is under the authority of the husband
who may manage and make decisions on without the consent of his

Cote d’Ivoire
Key institution Ministry of the Family, Women, and Children
Married women do not have the same rights as married men to own,

(Law on Marriage, art. 79). However, spousal consent is required for
major transactions (Law on Marriage, art. 81). The law provides for
joint land titling for land used or acquired by informal unions (Law on
Land rights Land, art. 10).
Unmarried women have the same rights as unmarried men to own,

non-land assets (Constitution, art. 11). After divorce or separation,
women and men share equal rights with regards to owning, using,
making decisions and using as collateral land, property and other non-
land assets (Law on Marriage, art. 108).

and to obtain credit (no restriction found).

Democratic Republic of Congo
Key institution The Ministry of Gender, Family Affairs and Children
According to the state’s Constitution, women and men are equally
guaranteed the right to property in accordance with law or custom,
and no citizen shall be deprived of their rightful property (Article34,
2011). Taken together with the law that prohibits discrimination
against women, this requires the government to ensure women
property rights both under statutory and customary law (Art. 14,
2011).In principle, the Constitution recognizes customary law, but
only to the extent that it does not contradict the Constitution.
Land rights Under statutory law, no distinction is made in the provision of land
rights between women and men (Land Law 1973). For married
persons, the state passed the Family Code in 1987 which outlines
three property regimes which allow for equal property ownership
rights for husbands and wives. These include the Separation of
Property (where each spouse keeps their own property); Communal
Acquisitions (where each spouse keeps the property they acquired
before the marriage, but share the property acquired during the
marriage); and Universal Community Property (where both spouses
share the property acquired before and during the marriage) (Family
Code, Arts. 487-537, 1987).
Amendments to the Family Code eliminate the need for a married
woman to obtain her husband’s permission to engage in any legal act
(Law 16-008, 2016). In principle, the amendment allows women the
right to open individual bank accounts as well as access formal
financial services such as a line of credit or financial loan. Moreover,
the government enacted microfinance legislation which guarantees
the right of each citizen to access microfinance services without any
discrimination, stressing that women specifically should have equal
Financial rights
rights to open bank accounts, access credit, and any other
microfinance service (Law 11/020, Art. 9-10, 2011).
Despite such laws that help promote women’s economic participation,
there is a general resistance toward women’s economic
empowerment in the country, even if it serves to enhance the well-
being the family unit (USAID, 2012). As such, women often
experienced economic discrimination, particularly in access to credit
(US Department of State, 2017; CEDAW, 2013). This is particularly so

Constitutional
Brazil’s Federal Constitution enshrines the principle of equality
equality
Women and men have the same rights to own, use and make decisions
over land (Constitution, art. 66, 69, 321). In particular, article 321 of
the Constitution recognises and guarantees “the right to property in
all of its forms, whether public, private, community, State,
associative, cooperative or mixed- economy”.
Since 2008, 60 100 hectares of land have been redistributed to 11 081
beneficiaries, 33% of which were women. Regarding land titling,
ancestral communities have received collective titles to about 500 000
hectares, benefiting almost 20 000 persons, 47% of which are women
Land rights (Deree, 2017).
However, there are some discrepancies between the Civil Code and
customary practices. Most land titles are attributed to the husband
and remain under their disposition. In rural areas, the
double signature for the acquisition of estate or property is not
common, which means that only the name of the buyer, often the
husband, is stipulated in the contract. Thus, women end up losing
access to land and property (FAO, Gender and Land Rights database).
No restrictions could be found regarding women’s right to open a bank
account or access credit. Besides, the right to obtain loans and
mortgages is guaranteed by article 375 of the Constitution in relation
to the right to a healthy environment and decent housing (CEDAW,

Gabon
Key institution The National Support Centre for Women's Organizations in Gabon
The legal framework provides married/unmarried women with the
same rights as married/unmarried men to own, use, make decisions
and use as collateral land, property and non-land assets. The Civil
Code establishes that each spouse can administer and enjoy his own
goods (buildings and non-buildings) and can dispose of it as they see
fit (art. 340). The right to property is enshrined in the Constitution,
establishing that no one can be deprived of his/her right to property
(art. 1-10). After divorce or separation, the law provides equally for
women and men in terms of matrimonial regimes and the separation
Land rights
of goods (Civil Code, art. 305). The law provides for joint land titling
by married couples (Law on the regime of land ownership, art. 52).
However, the Civil Code includes a discriminatory provision
establishing that marital property is administered by the husband (art.
335). The husband has to seek the consent of his wife regarding
decisions for the marital property, such as to dispose of the marital
property, even for the establishment of children, to earn from the
rent or to use marital property as collateral (Civil Code, art. 336).
The Civil Code establishes that a married woman who works can open
a bank account on her own and administer and enjoy the income she
earns (art. 262). The Civil Code stipulates that a married woman can
open a bank account without the signature of her husband but the
Financial rights husband must be notified of the opening of the bank account and he
has to give permission for debit (art. 257). The legal framework
provides married and unmarried women with the same rights as
married and unmarried men to obtain credit (African Union
Commission, 2015).

Indonesia
Key institution Ministry of Women Empowerment and Child Protection
Married and unmarried women have the same rights as men to own,
use, make decisions and use as collateral land and non-land assets
(Civil Code, Article 570; Marriage Law, Article 35; Constitution, Article
28H(4)). The default marital property regime is partial community of
property (Marriage Law, Articles 35 and 36) and both spouses must
agree in the administration of marital property (Marriage Law, Article
36(1)).
Land rights
Although the law formally adopts the concept of joint ownership of
property purchased during marriage or marital property, only few
parcels of land are registered in the joint name of husband and wife.
It is customary for the husband to register marital property in his name
(ADB, 2016), combined by the fact that there is little awareness that
title certificates for marital property can be issued in the name of
both spouses.
No legal restriction on married women’s rights to open a bank account
at formal financial institution could be located. However, Article 108
of the Civil Code creates a barrier to the acquisition of assets, as it
prevents married women from executing a deed or agreement on their
Financial rights own behalf and from receiving any payment from the latter without
consent of the husband.Although recent amendments to the law have
extended the same co-signing requirement to husbands (CEDAW,
2011, p.54), the equality guaranteed by the law is not always enforced
consistently (CEDAW, 2012).

Women are reported to have benefited from increasing rates of
female and joint land titling (ADB, 2012). The nation-wide process of
land mapping, registration and titling is still ongoing though, meaning
that women and men risk eviction or expropriation without
compensation if they do not hold a formal land title (ADB, 2012).
Matrimonial property is divided equally among spouses after divorce,
unless the dissolution of the marriage was caused by a fault
committed by one spouse, in which case this spouse only receives one
third of the matrimonial property. This rule is nuanced in the event
that the divorced couple has minor children, in which case the court
may award a bigger share to the parent to whom child custody is given
(Family law art. 28). The Land law is silent on land division and use
among spouses after divorce.
The banking laws of Lao PDR (e.g. 1995 Law on the Bank of Lao PDR,
2007 Law on commercial banks, 2012 Decree on microfinance
institutions) provide women with the same right as men to open bank
accounts and access credit, regardless of their marital status. The
microfinance sector is still nascent though and only a few commercial
banks and microfinance institutions operate outside the urban centres
Financial rights (GIZ, 2017). This limits the possibility for rural women to access
finance, who are already disadvantaged in accessing market
information due to their low levels of literacy and Lao language
proficiency, as well as traditional norms limiting women’s mobility
(ADB, 2012). Women therefore usually access capital via their
husbands who have greater financial literacy and a better ability to
understand formal banking procedures (ADB, 2012).
CEDAW The CEDAW was ratified on 14 August 1981.
CERD The CERD was ratified on 22 February 1974.
Liberia
Key institution The Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection
According to the Liberian Constitution, “every person shall have the
right to own property alone as well as in association with others”. This
law ensures that women have the same rights as men to individually
own, manage and use both land and non-land assets (Liberian
Land rights
Constitution, 1987). These privileges are also extended to married
women and men, allowing married persons “powers as though
unmarried” to hold property individually or jointly (Domestic
Relations Law, 1973; Descendants Estates Law, 1973).
E Co. 141

--- Table 1 on Page 280 ---
 |  |  | Women are reported to have benefited from increasing rates of
female and joint land titling (ADB, 2012). The nation-wide process of
land mapping, registration and titling is still ongoing though, meaning
that women and men risk eviction or expropriation without
compensation if they do not hold a formal land title (ADB, 2012).
Matrimonial property is divided equally among spouses after divorce,
unless the dissolution of the marriage was caused by a fault
committed by one spouse, in which case this spouse only receives one
third of the matrimonial property. This rule is nuanced in the event
that the divorced couple has minor children, in which case the court
may award a bigger share to the parent to whom child custody is given
(Family law art. 28). The Land law is silent on land division and use
among spouses after divorce.
Financial rights |  |  | The banking laws of Lao PDR (e.g. 1995 Law on the Bank of Lao PDR,
2007 Law on commercial banks, 2012 Decree on microfinance
institutions) provide women with the same right as men to open bank
accounts and access credit, regardless of their marital status. The
microfinance sector is still nascent though and only a few commercial
banks and microfinance institutions operate outside the urban centres
(GIZ, 2017). This limits the possibility for rural women to access
finance, who are already disadvantaged in accessing market
information due to their low levels of literacy and Lao language
proficiency, as well as traditional norms limiting women’s mobility
(ADB, 2012). Women therefore usually access capital via their
husbands who have greater financial literacy and a better ability to
understand formal banking procedures (ADB, 2012).

There is however a gap in the law that leaves women in consensual
informal or de-facto unions unprotected. In these cases, property
(even if jointly acquired), is assumed to belong to the man in these
unions because property rights are most often deeded under the

right to use land by virtue of affiliation with a customary group.
While women and men are afforded the same rights to open a bank
account and obtain credit, equal access among them to formal
financial resources is debatable. Several factors limit women’s access
to credit including: low levels of financial literacy, lack of collateral,
Financial rights the perception by some financial institutions that women pose a
higher risk, or corruption that at times comes in the form of sexual
assault or exploitation when women apply for a loan (IFC, 2014). As
such, women have relied on informal lines of credit such as credit or
loan clubs, otherwise known as susus (IFC, 2014).

Zambia
Key institution Ministry of Gender and Child Development
In Zambia, there is a two-tier system of land ownership; it may be
administered under statutory and customary tenure (CEDAW, 2010).
Under statutory law, unmarried and married women have the same
rights as men to own, use, make decisions over land and non-land
assets and use as collateral. Customary lands are governed by
traditional authorities and only men have the right to own and power
to dispose of property; wife or children may have access to it (CEDAW,
2010). Customary land accounts for the majority of total (96%)
whereas the remaining 6% are state lands (Centre On Housing Rights
Land rights
And Evictions, 2004). Therefore, most of the people in Zambia are
subjected to customary law.
The Zambia National Agriculture Investment Plan 2014-2018 provides
that at least 30% of beneficiaries shall be women (Ministry of
Agriculture and Livestock, 2013). It recognises the dual role of women
in both agricultural production and nutrition and highlights that
adequate support services may lead to positive outcomes.

Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
10. Conclusion and recommendations
This gender assessment has demonstrated that considering gender differences in the use of, access
to, and benefits from commodity supply chains forest landscapes can lead to more fair and
effective design of interventions and institutional arrangements. This is because gender-
differentiated tasks and responsibilities in commodity supply chains and the generation of income
often mean that women and men have different needs, opportunities, priorities, and concerns.
Although women tend to commercialize forest products less than men, the sale of forest products
can be an essential source of cash income for women, who lack many of the opportunities for
generating cash income commonly available to men. However, women’s role in agriculture and
their vulnerability to the impacts of land degradation are usually neglected.
The &Green Fund, focused on transitioning global supply chains from extractive to truly
sustainable blueprints recognizes that gender mainstreaming can maximize program results and
successes in addressing deforestation in many countries. In doing so, the Fund aligns with GCF’s
private sector and financing strategies. The climate fund recently adopted two new decisions
intended to reduce global emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, as well as to
support forest restoration and conservation in developing countries through:
• Improved role in financing development of policies and preparatory activities in
developing countries; and
• Improved policy related to making payments for verified emission reductions achieved
through such policies and measures.
The Fund will scale a portfolio of investments delivering quantifiable social, forest and climate
benefits as well as solid, risk-adjusted returns for investors. One of the pathways to achieve these
benefits will be through diminishing gender inequality through the invested portfolio. In principle,
&Green will tackle gender inequalities in three ways: understanding the gendered division of
labour, decision making process and access to financial services; drawing action plans specific to
the local context; and enhancing cooperation in local communities and raising awareness of
women’s empowerment.
If approved, the Fund will take the following approach to addressing gendered barriers:
• The &Green Fund’s Gender Approach will provide a framework to accelerate gender-
transformative and gender-sensitive (as appropriate for each Deal) investments through
the &Green Fund structure.
• The Gender Approach will be mobilized through the Environment and Social Action Plans
(ESAPs) – which are strict environmental and social safeguarding covenants that are
conditions of the loan contracts of the &Green Fund. The Gender Analysis has influenced
the overall logical framework (in Section E of this Funding Proposal) and has identified
entry points for the chosen paradigm shift pathway to deliver gender and social co-
benefits, which will be detailed project-level investment stage, as reflected in the
Gender Action Plan (presented in Appendix A).

Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
Appendix B. Tentative gender and social
inclusion activities
At a fund level, &Green could be expected to engage in the following activities, based on
needs assessments:
• Capacity building of SAIL Ventures staff, through internal and external training
• Inclusion of the &Green gender approach in fundraising marketing materials
• Inclusion of the &Green gender approach in the Fund’s ESMS
• Implementation of the &Green gender approach in the fund’s investment processes
• Inclusion of gender disaggregated data in monitoring, reporting and communication
of the portfolio
• Publication of ESMS, which will have the gender analysis embedded, on the &Green
website
• Publication of Landscape Protection Plans (LPPs) and Environmental and Social
Action Plans (ESAPs), with inclusion of a gender lens, on the &Green website.
At a portfolio company level, &Green could be expected to engage in the following
activities, depending on the context and supply chain/s with the company/ies::
• Adoption of a gender lens throughout the investment process, as per the &Green
gender approach.
• Allocate Technical Assistance to gender-focused assessments as part of the due
diligence process
• Assess and actively pursue gender transformative investment opportunities,
working together with portfolio companies to achieve gender inclusion targets as
part of our transformational change ambitions
• Crowd in private sector financing for gender-sensitive and gender-transformative
investment opportunities
Options appraisal for gender activities, for companies (depending on their
context/business focus) as part of their ESAP in &Green’s future portfolio may include:
• Inclusion of women in smallholder supply chains
• Promotion of women entrepreneurs in the landscape
• Women-focused stakeholder engagement processes
• Women representation in governance structures
• Training producers on gender-balanced practices
• Training of households on (financial) decision-making, family planning, nutrition,
hygiene and other topics that may have a positive impact on gender equality.
• Development of policies related to gender equity, prevention of Gender-based
Violence and SEAH.
E Co. 159

Page 295
Annex 8 – Gender Assessment and Gender Action Plan – The &Green Fund
• Women representation in other decision-making bodies
• Assessment and creation of job opportunities for women
• Providing enabling conditions and facilities for women to engage in employment
opportunities
• Ensuring accessibility and safe workspace to encourage women’s participation
